sharjah/ib-online-tutor.programmesIntro: Sharjah schools run the IB in different shapes, and the programme your child is in decides what a session can usefully do. The three below cover almost every enquiry that reaches us from the emirate.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three or four of them at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject is graded 1 to 7 and the core adds up to three further points. The externally examined papers carry most of the weight in most subjects, but the internally assessed component is the part students most often leave until it is too late to rescue, and it is the part a tutor can legitimately help with earliest.
programmes.countryNote: Sharjah Diploma candidates sit the same papers as everyone else, in a hall booked by their own school. What differs here is supply: the emirate has far fewer Diploma cohorts than Dubai, so a student needing Higher Level Physics or Economics support often finds no subject specialist within reasonable travelling distance. Live video removes that constraint entirely.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria lettered A to D, each scored 1 to 8 rather than as a percentage. There is no single mark out of a hundred, which is why MYP reports confuse parents who are used to one. A criterion total is converted to a 1 to 7 grade using boundaries your school publishes in its assessment policy. The Personal Project runs through the final year.
programmes.countryNote: MYP students in Sharjah frequently arrive from a British or Indian curriculum partway through, and the criterion system is the first thing that trips them. A student who was accurate under a percentage regime can score poorly on Criterion C or D simply because nobody explained what the command verbs in the task sheet were asking for.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, organised around transdisciplinary themes rather than separate subject syllabuses, and assessed continuously rather than by examination. Support at this stage is mostly about underlying literacy and number fluency, and about the habits of recording and explaining that the Middle Years Programme will later assess formally. It is not exam coaching, and treating it as such tends to make a young student worse rather than better.
programmes.countryNote: Sharjah families moving a child from a Ministry-curriculum or Indian-curriculum primary into a PYP school usually need help with written explanation rather than content. The child can do the mathematics and cannot yet write down how they did it, which is the thing the programme actually assesses.

sharjah/ib-online-tutor.subjectsIntro: These are the IB subjects Sharjah families ask about most often. Each note says what the component actually tests and where the marks tend to go, because that is what a session is planned around.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebraic fluency carries the paper. Marks go missing on unstructured proof questions, on calculus applied inside an unfamiliar context, and on the long questions where method marks are available but the working is not legible enough to award them. The exploration needs a question narrow enough to be answered in twenty pages.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling and statistics dominate, with heavier calculator dependence than Analysis. Students lose marks interpreting output rather than producing it: a correct regression with no statement of what the gradient means in context earns less than it should. Higher Level adds graph theory and matrices, which arrive late and feel disconnected.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The written papers reward precise use of definitions and clean handling of units and uncertainties. Higher Level candidates typically lose marks in the extended-response items where a derivation is asked for and a description is given instead. The internal assessment stands or falls on whether the uncertainty analysis is genuine.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics are where the Higher Level gap opens. Most recoverable marks sit in the structured questions: correct chemistry written in a form the markscheme cannot credit, equations left unbalanced, state symbols omitted. Data-based questions need practice at reading a table before answering anything.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Volume of content tempts students into recall-only answers. The examiner is usually asking for a causal chain, and a list of correct facts in the wrong order scores poorly. Marks are regularly lost by answering a command term one step below the one printed on the paper.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams do a large part of the work and are frequently drawn without labelled axes or a stated initial equilibrium. Evaluation is the dividing line at the top of the markband: a student who explains two effects and stops will not reach it. The internally assessed commentaries need current, properly referenced articles.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study papers reward application to the stimulus rather than textbook recall. Students lose marks by naming a tool and not using it on the company in front of them. Quantitative items are small but reliably available, and are often skipped by candidates who assume the subject is entirely written.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The guided analysis rewards close work on how a text makes meaning, not a summary of what it says. Marks disappear into paraphrase. The individual oral needs a global issue narrow enough to be genuinely traced through both an extract and a work.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Studies have to be used as evidence for an argument, not recited. The common failure is a well-remembered study with no link back to the question's command term. Higher Level extensions and the research methods strand need separate practice from the content.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Paper 1 rewards precise algorithmic reasoning and clean pseudocode. Students who can write working code in an editor often lose marks on paper because their trace tables are incomplete. The solution development stage of the internal assessment needs planning months before it is due.

sharjah/ib-online-tutor.regionsIntro: Sharjah is not one commuting pattern but several, and the one your family lives in decides what time a session can realistically start. These notes are about logistics rather than geography.

regions.name: Al Majaz
regions.note: Dense, central and close to the Corniche. Many families here hold places at Dubai schools, which means a long inbound run on Al Ittihad Road in the late afternoon. A seven o'clock start holds up across a term far better than a five o'clock one.

regions.name: Al Taawun
regions.note: Sits on the Dubai boundary near Al Mamzar, so the school journey can be short in the morning and slow in the evening. Families here often prefer two shorter sessions a week to one long one, because the usable window is narrow.

regions.name: Al Khan
regions.note: Mixed residential blocks with a spread of school choices across both Sharjah and Dubai. Siblings in this area are frequently on different curricula, which tends to mean two separate tutoring plans rather than one shared slot.

regions.name: Muwaileh
regions.note: One of the emirate's strongest school clusters, with several large international campuses within a few minutes of each other. Because the schools are close, afternoon sessions starting at half past four are workable here in a way they are not elsewhere.

regions.name: University City
regions.note: Built around the higher-education campuses, with a population used to academic timetables. Diploma students here often want late-evening slots because they are working around extracurricular commitments rather than around traffic.

regions.name: Al Nahda
regions.note: Straddles the Sharjah-Dubai line, and the morning queue out of it is a daily fact of life. Evening sessions are the norm, and families frequently ask for a fixed weekly slot so that the rest of the week can be planned around it.

regions.name: Aljada
regions.note: A newer master-planned community with a younger school-age population, so enquiries here skew towards the Middle Years Programme rather than Diploma. Scheduling is easier than in the older districts because the commutes are shorter.

regions.name: Khor Fakkan
regions.note: On the east coast, separated from the main emirate by mountain road. Private international provision is thin and the drive to a Sharjah city campus is not a daily proposition, which makes live video the only practical form of specialist support.

schoolClusters.city: Muwaileh, University City and Al Zahia
schoolClusters.note: The emirate's densest concentration of international campuses sits along this corridor. Curricula and programme authorisations change from year to year, so confirm what a school currently offers with the school itself or with SPEA rather than relying on any third-party list.

schoolClusters.city: Al Majaz, Al Qasimia and Al Taawun
schoolClusters.note: Older central districts with long-established schools and a high proportion of families whose children travel into Dubai. Session timing here is driven by the evening road rather than by the school bell.

sections.heading: What an IB online tutor in Sharjah is actually being asked to fix
paragraphs: An IB online tutor in Sharjah is hired, almost always, to close the distance between what a student knows and what an examiner can award. Those are different things, and the gap between them is where most of the recoverable marks in the Diploma sit. A student who can explain osmosis clearly at the dinner table and writes four disconnected true statements on the paper has a technique problem, not a knowledge problem, and reteaching the content will not touch it.

The first session is therefore spent on evidence rather than on syllabus. A marked script, a returned internal assessment draft, a mock paper with the examiner's annotations still on it: any of these tells a tutor more in ten minutes than a conversation about how the term has been going tells them in an hour. If none of that exists, the session starts with a short timed attempt at a past question so that there is something to look at.

From that, the work divides into three categories. There is content the student has not met or has met and forgotten, which is slow to fix and fixed by teaching. There is technique, which is fast to fix and consists mostly of learning what each command term obliges you to produce. And there is exam behaviour: how long is spent on the first question, whether the long-answer items are attempted at all, whether the calculator is being used to check or to think.

Most Sharjah students arriving with a predicted grade two below their target are losing marks in the second and third categories. That is good news, because those are the categories that move inside a term. Content gaps in a two-year course take longer and need the school's own teaching to do most of the work. A tutor who tells you otherwise in the first conversation has not looked at any evidence.
bullets: Bring a marked script to the first session if one exists
Technique and exam behaviour move faster than content
A predicted grade is a teacher's judgement, not a measurement
Ask what the tutor would work on first, and why

sections.heading: The six subject groups, and what each one actually assesses
paragraphs: Every Diploma candidate carries six subjects drawn from six groups, and the balance between externally examined and internally assessed work is different in each. Knowing which is which changes how a family should spend money on tutoring, because the two kinds of work have different deadlines and respond to different help.

External papers are sat in a hall, marked by an examiner the student will never meet, and cannot be revisited. Everything that can be done for them has to be done before the session. Internally assessed work is produced over weeks or months, marked by the subject teacher against published criteria, and then moderated. It is visible, it is fixable while it is still being written, and it is the part students most often postpone until the opportunity has gone.

The table below sets out the shape of each group. It is deliberately about form rather than content: what kind of thing the examiner receives, what the internal component looks like, and what a live video session does well with each. Confirm the current component structure for your child's specific subject against the subject guide the school holds, because the IB revises these on a rolling cycle and a subject that changed last year will not match an older summary.

One further consequence follows from the table, and it is a budgeting one. A family with a limited number of hours to buy should spend them first on whichever of their child's six subjects has the largest internally assessed share still unfinished, because that is the only part of the Diploma where help delivered today changes a mark that has not yet been awarded. External papers reward preparation too, but the preparation has to be spread across months to do anything, whereas an unfinished investigation responds to a single well-aimed hour.

sections.heading: Command terms are where Sharjah candidates lose the most recoverable marks
paragraphs: The IB publishes a defined list of command terms for every subject, and the examiner's markscheme is written against them. A question that says analyse does not accept a description. A question that says evaluate is not satisfied by two advantages and a disadvantage. This is not a stylistic preference; it is the difference between a mark being available and a mark being unavailable, and students lose them in quantity without ever being told that is what happened.

The pattern is consistent enough to be diagnosed from a single marked script. A student answering one level below the command term scores in the lower half of every extended item while getting the content entirely right, which produces exactly the profile that confuses parents: a child who clearly knows the subject and clearly is not being rewarded for it. It also produces a grade that will not move no matter how much revision is done, because revision addresses content and the problem is not content.

Fixing it is quick by the standards of the Diploma. A tutor takes four or five past questions on the same command term, has the student write only the opening sentence of each, and marks those sentences. Nothing else. After a fortnight of that, the student writes the right kind of thing by default. The table below lists the terms that cause the most damage and what each one obliges a candidate to produce.

One caution on using the table. Command terms are defined per subject, and the definition that matters is the one printed in the current guide for your child's course rather than a general gloss. The differences are small but they are real, and a student who learns a generic version will still occasionally write the wrong kind of answer. Ask the subject teacher for the list the school works from, and keep it on the desk during timed practice until it is no longer needed.

sections.heading: Higher Level against Standard Level: the hours before the rate
paragraphs: Families comparing tutoring costs usually compare hourly figures. The more consequential number is how many hours a subject needs, and that is set largely by whether the subject is taken at Higher Level. Higher Level courses carry more taught hours, extra topics, and in several subjects an additional paper, so the same weekly slot covers proportionally less ground.

The practical consequence is that a Higher Level subject in trouble rarely recovers on one session a fortnight. Either the frequency goes up or the scope comes down to a single named component. Trying to cover a whole Higher Level syllabus at low frequency produces sessions that feel productive and change nothing, because the student never spends long enough on any one weakness to stop making it.

Standard Level subjects behave differently. A Standard Level subject that is two grades below target is usually suffering from a small number of specific gaps, and those can be closed in a block of six to eight sessions rather than a continuing arrangement. It is worth being honest with a tutor about which of the two situations you are in, because the plans look nothing alike and buying the wrong one wastes a term.

The other decision hiding inside this is subject level itself. A student struggling badly in one Higher Level subject in DP1 may be better served by moving it to Standard Level than by buying tutoring for it, and that conversation belongs with the school's Diploma coordinator rather than with a tutor. A tutor whose advice is always more tutoring is not giving advice.

sections.heading: Internal assessment: what a tutor may do, and the line that does not move
paragraphs: Every Diploma subject has internally assessed work, and it is the single most common reason a Sharjah family contacts us. It is also the area where the market behaves worst. Services that offer to supply a completed exploration, investigation or essay are selling the student an academic misconduct finding, and the consequence of that finding falls entirely on the candidate, not on the service.

The honest version of the help is narrower and more useful. A tutor can teach the subject content the task depends on. A tutor can ask the questions that force a vague research question to become answerable. A tutor can read a draft the student has written and say which criterion is not yet being met and what kind of evidence would meet it. A tutor can mark the student's work against the published descriptors so the student can see the gap themselves.

What a tutor does not do is write, rewrite, restructure, or edit to completion any part of the work. They do not supply a research question. They do not provide data. They do not produce a model answer for the student to adapt. These are not cautious house rules; they are the boundary the IB sets, and a student who crosses it risks the whole Diploma.

There is also a timing point worth making plainly. The most valuable hour of coursework support is spent before anything is written, on the question itself. A badly framed question caps the mark no matter how well the rest is executed, and no amount of later feedback recovers it. Families who come to us in the week before a deadline are usually asking for the one thing nobody may do.

sections.heading: Who regulates your child's school, and why it matters to a tutoring plan
paragraphs: Private schools in the UAE are regulated at emirate level, and the body differs depending on where the campus sits. For Sharjah that is the Sharjah Private Education Authority. For Dubai it is the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, and for Abu Dhabi and Al Ain it is the Department of Education and Knowledge. In Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah the Ministry of Education supervises private schools directly, and in Ras Al Khaimah the Department of Knowledge does so.

This matters to Sharjah families more than it does elsewhere, because so many households here have children at schools in two different emirates. A family in Al Nahda may have one child at a Sharjah campus under SPEA and another at a Dubai campus under KHDA, with different inspection frameworks, different reporting cycles and different term dates. Two children, two calendars, one evening.

The federal position sits underneath all of this. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow one specified curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must otherwise adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is why a Sharjah school can run the IB and still timetable those subjects alongside it, and why a Diploma student here carries a load that an IB student in another country does not. Families planning tutoring sometimes forget to count those lessons when they work out how much time is actually left in a week.

There is a point about scope as well. The authority in Sharjah, and the equivalent body in Ras Al Khaimah, approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods for the schools they regulate. That is approval of schools, not of private tutors. No tutoring service in the UAE should describe itself as approved, accredited or licensed by any of these bodies unless it holds the specific permit in question and can show the number. Individual private tutors are covered by a separate route through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation.

sections.heading: Scheduling against a Sharjah evening
paragraphs: The most common reason a tutoring arrangement collapses in this emirate is not the tutor and not the student. It is a slot that was chosen optimistically in September and never survived contact with the road. A family agrees to five o'clock because that is when the child is theoretically home, discovers in week three that five o'clock is actually half past five on three weeks out of four, and by half term the session has become a source of friction rather than a fixed point in the week.

The fix is to choose the slot from the worst week rather than the best one. If the inbound journey from a Dubai campus can take ninety minutes in the second week of term, the session starts after that, not during it. A seven o'clock start that happens every week is worth considerably more than a five o'clock start that happens two weeks in three, because the value of weekly tutoring comes from the regularity rather than from any individual hour.

Two other patterns are worth knowing. Families with children at schools in different emirates often find that no single evening works for both, and run the two plans on different days rather than trying to stack them. And during Ramadan, timings shift across the whole emirate: school hours shorten, and many households move academic work to after Iftar. Agreeing in advance what the Ramadan schedule will be, rather than renegotiating it in the first week, keeps the arrangement intact through a month that otherwise tends to break it.

Weekend sessions are the other under-used option. Saturday mornings are quiet, nobody is tired, and a ninety-minute block on a Saturday frequently does more than two tired weekday hours. The trade-off is that it is the one slot families protect for other things, so it has to be agreed as a deliberate choice rather than a default.

sections.heading: Why these sessions run on video rather than in a Sharjah living room
paragraphs: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. Home visits are a service we run only in India, and every one of our UAE pages says so. For Sharjah the sessions on this page are one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, and the reasoning is worth setting out rather than asserting.

The first reason is supply. The emirate has a modest number of Diploma cohorts, which means the pool of people who have actually taught Higher Level Chemistry or Economics to IB candidates and who also live within a short drive of your address is small. Hiring by postcode means hiring from that small pool. Hiring over video means hiring the subject specialist and ignoring where they sleep, which for a Higher Level subject is the difference that decides the grade.

The second is cost and time. Published UAE market rates read in October 2026 put in-home one-to-one sessions meaningfully above online equivalents, and a visiting tutor's travel is paid for whether or not it is itemised on the invoice. In a corridor where an evening crossing between Sharjah and Dubai can take an hour each way, that premium is substantial and buys nothing academic.

The third is the record. A video session leaves a shared whiteboard, an annotated script and a written note behind it. A session in a living room leaves a memory of how it felt. For a parent who was not in the room, the first is checkable and the second is not. The comparison below sets the two formats side by side on the things that actually differ.

sections.heading: Getting started, and what we say when nobody is free
paragraphs: The process is short and deliberately unexciting. You tell us the subject, the level, the programme year and what the most recent piece of marked work looked like. We match a tutor who teaches that component. You take a free trial lesson. If it works you book a slot; if it does not you tell us and nothing further happens. No card details are taken before the trial.

The part worth stating plainly is what happens when the match is not available. Some Higher Level subjects have thin coverage at particular times of day, and the Diploma produces narrow requests: a student who needs Higher Level Mathematics Analysis specifically on Tuesday evenings is not an easy match. When we cannot cover it, we say so and give an honest estimate of when we can, rather than putting a general tutor in front of an examination-year student and calling it a match.

We will also say when tutoring is not the right purchase. A DP2 student six weeks from final papers with four subjects two grades below target does not have a tutoring problem that money solves; they have a triage problem, and the conversation that helps is about which two subjects to protect. A student whose difficulty is attendance, sleep or something outside the academic question is not helped by another hour of academic work either.

If you want to compare how the same service reads in another emirate before deciding, the equivalent pages for Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Al Ain, Ajman, Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah and Umm Al Quwain cover the same ground with local detail changed.

process.title: Tell us the component, not just the subject
process.description: The most useful opening message names the subject, the level, the programme year and the specific thing going wrong: a paper, a criterion, a type of question. That is enough to match a tutor properly the first time rather than after two mismatched sessions.

process.title: Send one piece of marked work
process.description: A marked script, a returned draft with comments, or a mock paper. One artefact tells a tutor more than a long conversation, and it means the free trial lesson starts on the actual problem rather than on finding out what it is.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: A full one-to-one session over live video with the matched tutor, with no card details taken beforehand. At the end you should be able to say what the tutor identified and what they proposed to do about it over the following month.

process.title: Fix a slot from your worst week
process.description: Choose the weekly time that survives a bad traffic week rather than the one that works on a good one. Regularity is where the value sits, and a slot chosen optimistically in September tends not to be there in November.

process.title: Read the notes, and change the plan if nothing moves
process.description: Each session leaves a written note. After six weeks there should be visible movement on the component being worked on. If there is not, the plan is wrong and should be changed, which is a more useful conversation than buying more of the same.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the component
whyPoints.description: A tutor is matched to the specific paper, criterion or skill that is costing marks, not to the subject in general. That is the difference between a session that reteaches what the student already knows and one that changes the next script.

whyPoints.title: Honest about coverage
whyPoints.description: When no specialist is free for a subject and time, we say so and give a realistic date. Substituting a general tutor into an examination-year Higher Level subject is the failure mode families complain about most, and it is avoidable.

whyPoints.title: Clear academic-honesty boundary
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach, question and give feedback on work the student has written. They do not draft, rewrite or supply coursework. That boundary is stated to the student in the first session so there is no ambiguity later.

whyPoints.title: Delivered where the specialist is
whyPoints.description: Sessions run over live video, so the tutor pool is not limited to people who live within driving distance of your address. For Higher Level subjects in a smaller emirate, that is the constraint that matters most.

whyPoints.title: Something written after every session
whyPoints.description: A short note saying what was worked on and what comes next. It is the only way a parent who was not in the room can tell whether the hour did anything, and it is what makes a six-week review possible.

faqs.question: Does an online IB tutor work as well for a Sharjah student as someone in the room?
faqs.answer: For most of what Diploma tutoring involves, yes, and for Higher Level subjects it usually works better. The substance of a session is a marked script, a worked solution and a conversation about why a mark was not awarded. All three transfer to a shared screen without loss. What video gives you that a local arrangement cannot is access to a tutor who has actually taught your child's component, rather than to the nearest person who covers the subject. In an emirate with a modest number of Diploma cohorts, that difference decides more than the format does.

faqs.question: My child is in DP1 at a Dubai school but we live in Sharjah. What time should sessions start?
faqs.answer: Choose the time that works in a bad traffic week rather than a good one. The inbound crossing in the late afternoon is unpredictable enough that a five o'clock slot will slip on a meaningful number of weeks, and a session that keeps moving stops being a fixed point. Most families in this position settle on seven o'clock or later on weekdays, or shift one of two weekly sessions to Saturday morning. The regularity matters more than the hour of day; a slot that happens every week beats an earlier one that happens sometimes.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the IB internal assessment without crossing an academic honesty line?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the boundary is clear enough to put in writing. A tutor can teach the content the task depends on, question a vague research question until it becomes answerable, read a draft the student has written and say which criterion is not yet met, and mark the work against the published descriptors. A tutor cannot write, rewrite, restructure or edit the work to completion, cannot supply the question, and cannot provide data. Any service offering finished coursework is creating a misconduct risk that falls on the student, not on them.

faqs.question: Which IB subjects are hardest to find a specialist for in Sharjah?
faqs.answer: Higher Level sciences and Higher Level Mathematics Analysis and Approaches are the narrowest, followed by subjects with small cohorts such as Computer Science, Psychology and the arts. The reason is arithmetic rather than anything about the emirate: fewer Diploma cohorts means fewer people locally who have taught the course at Higher Level. This is the clearest argument for video delivery. Searching by distance returns a short list sorted by proximity; searching by component returns a short list sorted by whether the person has taught it.

faqs.question: What does a command term actually have to do with my child's grade?
faqs.answer: More than almost anything else that can be fixed quickly. The IB publishes defined command terms and the markscheme is written against them, so a question asking a student to evaluate is not satisfied by a description, however accurate. Students who answer one level below the term printed on the paper score in the lower half of every extended question while getting the content right. That produces a grade that does not move with revision, because revision addresses content and the problem is not content. It is usually diagnosable from one marked script.

faqs.question: How many sessions does a Diploma subject usually need before anything changes?
faqs.answer: If the issue is technique rather than content, six to eight weekly sessions is normally enough to see movement on the component being worked on, provided the student is also doing the written work between sessions. Content gaps across a two-year Higher Level course take longer, and most of that work has to be done by the school's own teaching. Anyone who promises a specific grade shift in a specific number of hours is guessing. What you can reasonably ask for is visible change in the thing being targeted, reviewed after six weeks.

faqs.question: Is a private tutor working with my child in Sharjah required to hold a permit?
faqs.answer: Individuals providing private tuition in the UAE need a private tutor work permit, introduced through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Ask a tutor directly, and apply or verify through MoHRE's own service channels.

faqs.question: Is IB Gram approved by SPEA or by the IB?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from the Sharjah Private Education Authority, any other emirate regulator, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge or Pearson, and no page on this site should be read as claiming otherwise. Those bodies regulate schools and qualifications, not tutoring services. What we can tell you is what the regulators do, where to verify a school's standing, and what the permit position is for individual private tutors in the UAE. Treat any tutoring service describing itself as regulator-approved with real caution.

faqs.question: My child is moving from MYP into DP1 next year. Is it worth starting now?
faqs.answer: The summer between MYP 5 and DP1 is one of the better times to use a small number of sessions, because the work is cheap to do and expensive to skip. The gap is not mainly content; it is the shift from criterion-based tasks with published descriptors to timed papers written against command terms. Four to six sessions spent on that transition in a Higher Level subject the student intends to take does more than the same sessions spent in a panic in DP2. It also makes the first set of DP1 assessments readable rather than alarming.

faqs.question: What happens to tutoring during Ramadan in Sharjah?
faqs.answer: School hours shorten across the emirate and most households move academic work later in the day, so sessions commonly shift to after Iftar for the month. The arrangement that survives is the one agreed in advance: a fixed alternative time set before Ramadan starts, rather than a renegotiation in the first week when everybody's routine is already unsettled. Some families reduce to one session a week for the month and add a block afterwards. Both work. What does not work is leaving it undecided and losing four weeks.

faqs.question: How do I tell whether the tutoring is working if I was not in the room?
faqs.answer: By looking at artefacts rather than at impressions. After each session there should be a written note naming what was worked on. Over six weeks there should be marked work showing the targeted problem happening less often: fewer command-term substitutions, uncertainty analysis actually present, evaluation paragraphs reaching a verdict. A school report arrives too late and measures something broader. Ask for the note after every session from the beginning, and set a six-week point at which you decide whether the plan continues unchanged.

faqs.question: We live in Khor Fakkan. Is online tutoring realistic from the east coast?
faqs.answer: It is the only realistic form of specialist support there, and it works without compromise. Private international provision on the east coast is thin, and the mountain road to a Sharjah city campus is not a daily journey for a tutoring session. A live video lesson removes the problem entirely: the tutor is wherever they are, the student is at a desk at home, and the session starts on time regardless of the road. Connection quality matters more than distance, and a wired connection or a seat near the router is worth arranging.

faqs.question: Should we use the same tutor for two of my child's Diploma subjects?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it is worth asking, but it should not be the deciding factor. A tutor with genuine depth in two related subjects at the level required can carry both, which simplifies scheduling and billing. A tutor who covers two subjects because the family asked rather than because they teach both at that level is a worse outcome than two separate matches. For Higher Level subjects, depth should win over convenience every time. For a Standard Level subject alongside a Higher Level one, a single match is more often workable.

faqs.question: What does the free trial lesson actually involve?
faqs.answer: A full one-to-one session over live video with the tutor matched to the subject and component, not a sales call. The tutor looks at whatever marked work you have sent, works on it with the student for the session, and at the end sets out what they think the problem is and what they would do about it over the following month. No card details are taken beforehand. If you decide not to continue, you tell us and nothing further happens. If you do continue, the slot is fixed from the following week.

faqs.question: Does a predicted grade from the school mean the final grade is settled?
faqs.answer: No. A predicted grade is a teacher's professional judgement based on the evidence available at the time, and it is used for university applications rather than as a forecast of the outcome. Grades move in both directions between prediction and final results, particularly where internally assessed work is still unfinished or where a student's technique on timed papers changes. It is a useful signal about where attention is needed. It is not a measurement, and treating it as one makes families either complacent or alarmed without cause.

sharjah/ib-online-tutor.closingBody: If you are weighing up an IB online tutor in Sharjah, the most useful thing you can do before spending anything is to find one marked piece of work and look at where the marks actually went. Send it with the subject, the level and the programme year, and we will match a tutor who teaches that component and arrange a free trial lesson over live video. If we cannot cover it properly at the time you need, we will tell you that instead of putting someone approximate in front of your child. Either way you will know more about the problem than a termly report told you.

sharjah/ib-tutor.tutorsIntro: Each tutor below is listed against the components they teach rather than against a subject label, because the useful match is at component level. A candidate losing marks in extended response needs someone who marks extended response, not someone who happens to list the subject.

intro.heading: Name the fault before you buy the hours
paragraphs: Most searches for an IB tutor in Sharjah start from a number: a 4 where a 6 was expected, a report comment about effort, a mock percentage that does not match what the household sees at the kitchen table. The number is a symptom. What decides whether tutoring works is what is underneath it, and there are not very many possibilities. Diploma candidates lose recoverable marks in a small set of identifiable ways, and each of those ways needs a different month of work.

The five that account for most of the loss are these. The candidate does not know a specific piece of content, which is the slowest to fix. The candidate knows the content but answers a different question from the one asked, usually by misreading a command term, which is the fastest to fix and transfers to every paper in the subject. The candidate runs out of time and leaves marks on the table. The candidate describes where the paper asked them to analyse or evaluate. And the candidate's internally assessed work is structured in a way that caps the criterion marks regardless of the quality of the thinking.

Those five are not interchangeable and they do not cost the same to put right. A candidate whose script shows command-term faults and timing faults can move substantially in six weeks. A candidate whose script shows missing foundations needs a longer plan and deserves to be told so before anyone takes a booking. The only way to tell which you have is to look at a marked script, which is why the first fortnight here is diagnostic rather than instructional.

Sharjah adds its own constraints to the plan, and they are practical rather than academic. SPEA regulates private education in the emirate and, along with Ras Al Khaimah's authority, approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so curriculum approval and not just inspection sits at emirate level here. A large share of Sharjah households also send children into Dubai schools from Al Nahda and Al Majaz, which means the school day ends later than the timetable suggests and the earliest realistic session slot moves accordingly.

The rest of this page works through the five faults, the diagnostic that distinguishes them, the mandatory UAE subjects that sit alongside the Diploma in this emirate, the commute arithmetic that decides when a session can start, and what a tutor is and is not permitted to do with internally assessed work. The Diploma itself is reported out of 45 points, with up to 7 available in each of six subjects and up to 3 from the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay combination; confirm the current structure and the conditions for the award with your child's Diploma coordinator.
bullets: Five fault types, each identified from a marked script rather than a grade
A week-one diagnostic of four questions that separates them

sharjah/ib-tutor.programmesIntro: The IB continuum runs across three programmes and the faults above present differently in each. A Sharjah family is usually dealing with one of these three, and the right support is not the same in all of them.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, with no external examinations, so there are no marks to lose yet. What can go wrong is a gap in arithmetic fluency or written structure that stays hidden because the programme does not test it directly, then reappears as a pace problem in the Middle Years Programme.
programmes.countryNote: Sharjah families moving a child between schools, including into or out of a Dubai school, most often find the gap at this stage, because what two schools cover in the same year differs more than the programme name suggests. A short diagnostic block is worth more here than a term of general support.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Assessed against criteria written as descriptors rather than against mark schemes, which trains a particular habit: candidates learn to satisfy a descriptor in prose. The fault that carries into the Diploma is a weak instinct for command terms, because MYP criteria rarely punish answering a slightly different question.
programmes.countryNote: In this emirate the MYP years also carry the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies load alongside the programme, which makes a Sharjah MYP timetable genuinely fuller than its equivalent elsewhere. That matters when deciding how many extra weekly hours a child can absorb.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay, with internally assessed components completed across two years and written papers at the end. This is where all five fault types become expensive, because every one of them now converts directly into points on a 45-point scale.
programmes.countryNote: Sharjah Diploma candidates sit the same externally set papers as candidates anywhere else, which is the reassuring part: the assessment does not vary by emirate. What varies is the school's internal deadline calendar and the household's usable evening, and the plan is built around both.

sharjah/ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are the ones Sharjah families bring most often, described by the fault each one punishes hardest rather than by a syllabus summary. Confirm exact components and weightings in the current subject guide your child's school issues.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Punishes working omission above everything else. Candidates who reach correct answers by calculator and write nothing in between forfeit method marks they had earned. Proof questions are the second cluster, usually abandoned at the first line rather than attempted in parts.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Punishes failure to interpret. The computation is usually within reach; the marks go on choosing a model for a described situation and justifying it in words, which candidates trained purely on technique treat as optional commentary.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Punishes unstated assumptions and unquoted data. A candidate who understands the mechanism loses marks by describing a graph trend without citing values from it, or by omitting the uncertainty treatment the question expected.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Punishes command-term drift hardest of the three sciences. Observations given where explanations were asked for, and explanations given where justifications were asked for, cost marks on content the candidate knew perfectly.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Punishes imprecision. Terminology that is nearly right scores nothing, and data questions reward quoting figures rather than describing shapes. The volume of content also makes re-reading feel like progress when practice is what moves marks.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Punishes unfinished reasoning. Candidates define, explain and apply, then stop before the judgement the command term asked for. Diagram accuracy is the second recoverable block: axes, the correct shift, the new equilibrium marked.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Punishes generic answers. A response that would fit any organisation rather than the one in the case study sits in the lower bands, however well written. Correcting that habit is a few weeks of focused practice, not a content programme.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Punishes summary. Marks come from an argument about how a text produces meaning, supported by specific textual features, and candidates who retell content accurately still score low. Timed essays with annotated marking are the mechanism here.

subjects.name: Arabic and language acquisition subjects
subjects.description: Punishes unstructured preparation. Productive skills respond to frequent short practice with correction, and candidates often arrive having revised vocabulary lists rather than having rehearsed the assessed tasks themselves.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Punishes description without evaluation. Study recall is finite and quick to finish; the marks sit in saying what a study fails to show, which is a drillable move rather than additional content.

sharjah/ib-tutor.regionsIntro: In this emirate the question that decides a schedule is where the school is, not where the home is, because a large share of Sharjah households travel into Dubai for school. These are the communities families book from, with the slot each one realistically supports.

regions.name: Al Nahda
regions.note: The heaviest Dubai-bound commute in the emirate. Where a child attends school across the boundary, arrival home after 16:30 is normal in term time, which makes 18:00 the earliest slot that is not taken out of homework.

regions.name: Al Majaz
regions.note: Central, with schools both locally and across the boundary, so households in the same building keep very different schedules. A fixed weekly slot agreed once in September saves renegotiating it every month.

regions.name: Muwaileh
regions.note: Dense school provision within a few minutes, so the commute is short and the constraint is activity load rather than travel. Twice-weekly short sessions fit this pattern better than one long block.

regions.name: Al Zahia and Al Mamsha
regions.note: Newer communities with young Diploma cohorts and thin local specialist supply, particularly at Higher Level in the sciences. The widening of the tutor pool matters more here than the timing does.

regions.name: Aljada
regions.note: A growing population with a mix of local and Dubai schooling, and enough internal amenity that evenings fill with activities. Families here most often ask for a 19:30 or later slot and use the lesson recording.

regions.name: University City
regions.note: Household routines are shaped by university timetables as well as school ones, which makes weekend morning sessions unusually workable compared with the rest of the emirate.

regions.name: Kalba and Khor Fakkan
regions.note: On the east coast, under the same regulator but a long way from the city. A visiting arrangement is not realistic from here at all, and video delivery is the only route to a Higher Level specialist.

regions.name: Al Qasimia and Al Juraina
regions.note: Established, central and close to several large schools, with group tuition easy to find locally. The useful question here is what individual diagnosis adds to what is already available nearby.

schoolClusters.city: Al Majaz, Al Taawun and Al Khan
schoolClusters.note: The city-side cluster, where IB and British-curriculum provision sits close together and a household can realistically choose between them. Students we support attend schools in this cluster.

schoolClusters.city: Al Nahda and the Dubai boundary
schoolClusters.note: Households here commonly attend school across the emirate boundary, which puts them under a different regulator for school matters while living under SPEA's jurisdiction for everything else. The practical effect is on timing rather than on curriculum.

sharjah/ib-tutor.modesIntro: Support for a Diploma candidate in this emirate takes three shapes, chosen by which fault the script shows rather than by preference. All run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

modes.title: Fault-targeted block
modes.description: Six to eight weeks aimed at one named fault in one subject, with the same question type practised, marked and re-practised until the fault stops appearing. This is the shape for command-term drift, timing collapse and description-instead-of-analysis, all of which are habits rather than knowledge gaps.
bullets: One fault, one subject, one question type at a time
A marked example in every session, from the candidate's own attempt
The fault tracked by count, not by impression

modes.title: Content repair block
modes.description: The slower shape, for a genuine knowledge gap. Topics are sequenced by dependency rather than by syllabus order, so a prerequisite is never taught after the thing that needs it. Expect this to run longer than families hope, and expect to be told so before it starts rather than during it.
bullets: Topics sequenced by dependency, not by the order of the subject guide
A short retention check on earlier topics in every session
Written honesty about how many weeks the gap needs
Reviewed monthly against a timed section rather than against coverage

modes.title: Component coaching on internally assessed work
modes.description: Support on the student's own internally assessed work: understanding what each criterion rewards, reading a draft the student wrote and asking questions about it, and planning time against the school's internal deadlines. The student writes every word. No text is supplied and nothing is edited to completion.

sections.heading: The five faults, and what each one costs to fix
paragraphs: A direct answer first. Diploma candidates in this emirate lose recoverable marks in five identifiable ways: missing content, command-term misreading, timing collapse, description where analysis was required, and internally assessed work structured so that criterion marks are capped. Each is visible on a marked script, each needs a different intervention, and they cost between one session and several months to address. Buying hours without knowing which one you have is the most common way tutoring money produces nothing.

The reason this matters more than subject choice is that four of the five transfer. A candidate who learns to read command terms properly improves in every written paper they sit, not only in the subject where the fault was diagnosed. A candidate who fixes timing improves across the board. A candidate who learns to finish an analytical move rather than stopping at explanation carries that into every essay-based subject. Only missing content is genuinely local to one topic in one subject, and it is also the most expensive thing on the list.

So the sequencing is not negotiable here. Two timed sections are attempted, marked against the published scheme, and the losses are categorised before a teaching plan exists. If the categories come back dominated by content, the honest conversation is about months rather than weeks. If they come back dominated by the four transferable faults, a six-week block can do a great deal and the family should be told that too.

The table below is the categorisation format. The counts are yours once the first scripts are marked; what the table fixes is the vocabulary, so that a conversation with the school and with a tutor uses the same words.

sections.heading: The week-one diagnostic: four questions that separate the faults
paragraphs: Before any teaching, four questions are put to the candidate's own work, and the answers are what the plan is built from. The first: on the questions the candidate got wrong, did they know the content? If the answer is yes on most of them, the problem is not knowledge and a content course would be the wrong purchase. This single question redirects more plans than any other.

The second: did the answer address the command term the question used? Candidates are asked to read the question aloud, say what the command term requires, and then compare that to what they wrote. The gap between the two is often visible to the student before the tutor says anything, which is useful, because a fault the candidate can see is a fault they can start correcting without supervision.

The third: where on the paper did the marks stop? A script that is strong until the last two questions has a timing fault, not a knowledge one, and the fix is a question order and a watch rather than a syllabus. The fourth: in internally assessed work, which criterion is capping the mark, and is the cap caused by structure or by content? Those are different problems and only one of them is addressed by more research.

Each answer has a different cost attached, which is why the diagnostic is worth buying on its own. A family can take the four answers, the marked scripts and the categorised losses to the school, decide nothing further, and still be better placed than they were. That is a legitimate outcome and it is offered as one.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the Diploma
paragraphs: A Diploma timetable in the UAE is not the Diploma timetable published in international guides, and families who have moved here from elsewhere are often surprised by the difference. Private schools in the Emirates are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Those subjects run alongside the licensed international curriculum rather than instead of part of it, which makes a UAE school week genuinely fuller.

The detail of how that is implemented is published most fully by Dubai's regulator, and although SPEA governs Sharjah schools the shape is instructive. KHDA requires separate classes by group for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, stating that combined classes for Arabs and non-Arabs are strictly prohibited because of different curriculum expectations and language of instruction, and that mandatory-subject instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit with a recommended minimum lesson length of 25 minutes. It also requires that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold the appropriate approval from the regulator to teach those subjects.

For a tutoring plan, three consequences follow. First, the available weekly hours for additional support are fewer than an international timetable would suggest, so a plan built on four extra hours a week may not be physically possible. Second, Arabic is an examinable subject with its own assessed tasks and responds to frequent short practice rather than to vocabulary revision. Third, for the mandatory subjects the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry is prohibited, so support there means working with the school's own material rather than substituting anything for it.
Confirm your own school's arrangements with the school, because implementation differs by emirate and by cohort, and SPEA rather than KHDA is the approving authority for schools in Sharjah.

sections.heading: SPEA, curriculum approval, and what it does not mean
paragraphs: The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in the emirate, and its powers go further than inspection. Along with Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge, SPEA approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. That is a meaningful difference from a purely inspecting regulator: in this emirate the approval of what is taught and what is charged sits at emirate level, which is why school-level answers to curriculum questions here often reference the authority directly.

Across the country the regulator map is complete and worth knowing, because Sharjah families frequently have children in schools in more than one emirate. Dubai schools answer to KHDA, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education there. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain schools answer to ADEK, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in that emirate. Ras Al Khaimah has its Department of Knowledge. The Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

What none of that means is that any tutoring provider is approved, accredited, licensed or endorsed by any of these bodies. IB Gram holds no such status and claims none. The phrase to be wary of in this market is a provider describing its tutors as approved by a regulator, because that is a specific factual claim about a specific body and it can be checked with that body. A regulator oversees schools; it does not certify private tutors by brand.

What does apply to individuals is the permit regime. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit, under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit is granted free of charge for two years. Those giving private lessons without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount is quoted here.

sections.heading: The Sharjah commute, and when a session can realistically start
paragraphs: A schedule that ignores the school run in this emirate will be renegotiated within a fortnight. A substantial number of Sharjah households attend school across the Dubai boundary, and the return journey in term time is the single largest determinant of when a child is capable of useful work. A 16:00 finish on a timetable can mean a 17:15 arrival home from Al Nahda, which means a 17:00 session slot does not exist in practice however willingly it was booked.

The pattern varies by community and it is worth being specific. Households using local Sharjah schools in Muwaileh or Al Qasimia generally have short runs and can genuinely start at 17:00. Al Nahda and Al Majaz households going into Dubai usually cannot start before 18:00 in term time. East coast families in Kalba and Khor Fakkan have long local runs and often prefer weekend mornings entirely. University City households, shaped by university schedules as well as school ones, are the group most able to use Saturday mornings.

Session length follows from this rather than from a standard product. Where a child arrives home late and tired, two short sessions in a week beat one long one, and the long one will quietly become a shorter one anyway. Where the run is short, a single longer session can work for content repair, which needs continuity. Fault-targeted work prefers frequency in every case, because habits change by repeated correction rather than by exposure.

Ramadan shifts the whole pattern to post-Iftar for many households, typically from around 21:00, with shorter and more frequent sessions. Study leave inverts it again: mornings become the right slot because papers are sat in the morning. The schedule is agreed against the family's real weeks before the content plan is written.

sections.heading: What the first month changes, and what it does not
paragraphs: In the first month, three things change and they are all observable. The fault count falls: whatever was named in week one appears less often in marked work by week four, and it is counted rather than described. The candidate's own account of what a question is asking becomes more accurate, which you can hear at home without reading any script. And the paper gets finished, where timing was the fault, because a question order was built and rehearsed.

What does not change in a month is a grade, and nobody should claim otherwise. A reported grade moves when enough marks move across enough papers, and a single assessment result bounces for reasons unconnected to teaching: the paper was harder, the topic distribution favoured the candidate or did not, the week was bad. What a tracked fault count shows is whether the specific thing being worked on is improving, which is a claim that can be checked rather than asserted.

That distinction is also what makes the evidence useful outside the house. A school asked to look again at a prediction will engage with a marked script and a fault count more readily than with a report of improvement, because both are the kind of material teachers produce themselves. The school still owns the prediction; what changes is what it has in front of it.

If the month shows no movement in the named fault, that is information too, and it should produce a change of plan rather than a renewal. Sometimes the fault was misdiagnosed. Sometimes the match is wrong. Sometimes the right answer is fewer subjects supported, more intensively. Those are all better outcomes than quietly continuing.

sections.heading: What a tutor may touch, and what belongs to the student alone
paragraphs: Internally assessed work is the student's own and the boundary around it does not move. A tutor explains what each criterion rewards, discusses a plan, asks questions about a draft the student produced, and points at the criterion a paragraph is currently failing to satisfy. The student writes every word, chooses the topic, runs the investigation and reaches the conclusions. No text is supplied, nothing is edited to completion, and no model is handed over to be adapted.

The reason to be explicit is the market. At least one provider in this region openly sells completed internal assessments, and the consequence of using such a service falls on the candidate, not the seller, as a malpractice matter with their own school and board. A family paying for legitimate coaching is entitled to know exactly where the line is before they ask a question that crosses it, and a tutor who cannot describe the line is not safe to buy from.

In practice the honest process leaves a trail, and the trail is the proof. The student sends what they wrote. The tutor returns questions and criterion references. Each version is kept with its date. If a Diploma coordinator asks how the work was supported, the answer is a folder rather than an assurance. That same trail is what protects the student if the question is ever asked formally.

Where a component is already submitted, the mark is fixed and further hours against it buy nothing. The honest recommendation at that point is to move the hours to the written papers, which is a smaller sale and the right one.

sections.heading: Why the sessions run on video, and what happens when nobody is free
paragraphs: Lessons for Sharjah families are delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with a shared whiteboard, the paper on screen and the session recorded so it can be rewatched. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Sharjah or anywhere else in the UAE; that service exists only in India. The case for it here rests on the fault list at the top of this page.

Four of the five faults are fixed by frequent short correction rather than by long exposure, and frequency is exactly what a travelling arrangement cannot provide. A visiting tutor in this emirate is typically quoted with a two-hour minimum because the journey has to be worth making, and market rates for in-home work run to AED 500 an hour with travel inside the fee. The same money spent on video sessions buys more sessions, spaced more usefully, which is the shape the work wants.

The second argument is the pool. A candidate losing marks in Higher Level Physics extended response needs a tutor who marks extended response in that subject, and the set of such people who can drive to Kalba on a Tuesday afternoon is close to empty. Removing the journey makes the match about the component. For families on the east coast and in the newer western communities, that is the difference between a specialist and whoever was available.

Coverage is disclosed rather than assumed. If nobody who teaches your child's exact component has hours in the window you need, you are told, and offered a named alternative with the trade-off stated: a specialist working Gulf Standard Time from another country, the subject split by component across two tutors with a single shared record, hours reallocated to a subject where the match is right, or a later start. Filling the slot with a generalist would make the fault list on this page undiagnosable.
