sharjah/university-city.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover the subjects University City families ask about when a destination is already in view: both Diploma maths courses, Higher Level sciences, and the IGCSE subjects that keep a route open rather than the ones that merely improve a report.

intro.heading: Living next to the universities changes the question
paragraphs: University City is Sharjah's academic quarter, a belt of campuses and residential blocks east of Muwaileh where the University of Sharjah, the American University of Sharjah and several higher and technical institutions sit within a few minutes of each other. The households around them are unlike those in the coastal districts: faculty families, postgraduate families, staff housing, and families who moved here deliberately because the next stage of education is visible from the window.

That proximity shows up in the tutoring enquiry itself. Parents elsewhere ask how to lift a grade. Parents here tend to ask which subject combination keeps a particular degree available, and whether a given maths course will be accepted by a given faculty. It is a better question, and it is also a question that has to be asked at least two years before it becomes urgent, because the decisions it depends on are taken at the end of Year 11 and cannot be unwound in Year 13.

There is a second characteristic, and it is the one nobody says out loud. Academic households often contain somebody who could, in principle, teach the subject. A parent with a doctorate in chemistry can explain chemistry. What they usually cannot do is mark their own child's work to an examiner's standard without the relationship getting in the way, and the sessions where a parent teaches a teenager tend to end early and badly. Outsourcing the marking is not an admission of incompetence; it is a sensible division of labour.

The third feature is a genuine local supply of tutors. University students are explicitly eligible for the UAE private tuition work permit, and in a district built around campuses there are plenty of them. For primary and lower secondary support that is a reasonable and affordable option. For Higher Level Diploma subjects and for route advice it is a different requirement, and the honest distinction is worth making before money changes hands.

One more thing marks this district out. Because the campuses are visible and the destinations feel close, the risk is not complacency but over-concentration: a plan formed in Year 10 that every subject choice then serves, with no second door if the grade or the interest moves. Two of the three variables in any such plan sit outside the family's control, which is an argument for designing a subject set that keeps a second field live rather than for aiming harder at one.

IB Gram delivers lessons one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not visit homes in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service offered only in India. For a University City family the practical consequence is that the tutor is chosen for subject, level and route knowledge rather than for walking distance from a campus gate.

sharjah/university-city.programmesIntro: Three programmes matter to a household thinking about destinations. Each entry below focuses on the decisions inside the programme rather than on its philosophy, because decisions are what close or keep options open.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects chosen across subject groups, three normally at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Grades run 1 to 7 per subject with up to three further points from the core, giving a 45-point maximum. Higher Level choices, not the total, are what most faculties look at first.
programmes.countryNote: In University City the Diploma conversation is almost always about the Higher Level triple and the group five choice. A candidate who takes three Higher Level subjects unrelated to their intended field has a diploma and a problem, and the point at which that becomes fixable is the selection meeting at the end of Year 11, not the term before the exams.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten subjects examined at the end of Year 11, graded 9 to 1 or A* to G depending on the syllabus, with tiering in Cambridge maths and sciences. The subject set here does double duty: it is a qualification in its own right and the entry filter for sixth-form course selection.
programmes.countryNote: Dropping a subject in Year 10 to lighten a timetable is the decision most likely to close a route quietly. A candidate without a science at Extended tier, or without the maths tier a sixth form expects, can find a Higher Level door shut two years later. Check the sixth-form prerequisite before accepting a drop.

programmes.name: Advanced Level and Advanced Subsidiary
programmes.description: The alternative post-16 route, taken by candidates in British-curriculum schools, with linear examinations and no core components. It appears here because it is the other half of the equivalency rule for the British track, and because many University City families are comparing the two routes directly.
programmes.countryNote: The published equivalency guidance for the British track asks for one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade no lower than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, alongside the five GCSE or IGCSE subjects. That is the floor for equivalency and is not a university entry standard, which is a distinction families here are quick to grasp and slow to be told.

sharjah/university-city.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are the ones that come up when a destination is already in mind. Each entry names the part that matters for route-keeping rather than describing the syllabus.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The algebraic and calculus-heavy route, with proof, complex numbers and advanced calculus at Higher Level and an unseen problem-solving Paper 3. This is the course that quantitative degree programmes most often assume, which is why the choice is strategic rather than a matter of preference.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Calculator-permitted throughout, with statistics and modelling carrying the weight and interpretation in context carrying the marks. Suited to candidates heading towards social sciences, design and business, and accepted by many but not all quantitative programmes.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The Higher Level course is the standard prerequisite assumption for engineering, and fields and circular motion are where capable candidates stall because the algebra and the reasoning must run together.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Commonly required at Higher Level for medicine and the life sciences. Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms carry the teaching load, and the internally assessed investigation decides a fifth of the grade.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-heavy, with marks lost to imprecise language rather than to ignorance. Examiners want the structure named, the mechanism linked and the direction stated, which is a writing discipline as much as a knowledge one.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and evaluation decide the grade. The portfolio of three commentaries based on published articles is where candidates lose marks for a poor article choice before any analysis begins.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Algorithmic thinking and the solution development component carry the difficulty. Candidates who code fluently still lose marks on documenting a design and justifying a data structure choice.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The individual oral and the guided analysis require a claim about how a text works. For second-language candidates the ideas are usually present and the argument scaffolding is not, which is the faster thing to fix.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580
subjects.description: Extended tier is the entry assumption for most post-16 maths routes, and the tier is fixed at the entry deadline months before the papers. This is the single most route-relevant decision in Year 10.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625
subjects.description: Keeping Extended physics open preserves the engineering and physical sciences route. The alternative-to-practical paper is the biggest source of avoidable loss, usually on control variables and repeat readings.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Up to three points between them, and an Extended Essay in the intended degree subject is a genuinely useful thing to have written. Support is question framing and feedback on the student's own drafts, never supplied prose.

sharjah/university-city.regionsIntro: University City sits inland at the eastern end of the Sharjah school belt. These are the districts around it, described by the practical relationship rather than in isolation.

regions.name: Muwaileh
regions.note: Immediately west and the emirate's densest school district. Most University City school-age children attend a Muwaileh school, which means the two areas share mock windows and internal deadlines almost exactly.

regions.name: Al Zahia
regions.note: North-west, villas and townhouses, and a common destination for families who move out of campus-adjacent housing when a second child arrives. School arrangements usually survive the move.

regions.name: Aljada
regions.note: West towards the centre, newer and growing quickly. Families there compare notes with University City households at the same school gates, which is how route questions spread between the two districts.

regions.name: Sharjah Garden City
regions.note: South along the Al Dhaid road, villa-based and further out. Children from there are in the same classrooms but lose considerably more of the day to the commute.

regions.name: Al Nouf and Al Ramtha
regions.note: Established inland districts between University City and the older centre, with a mix of villa and apartment housing and shorter journeys into the school belt than the coastal areas have.

regions.name: Tilal City
regions.note: Further into the interior. A University City school day plus that commute makes Saturday morning the only realistic slot for long-form work such as Extended Essay drafting.

regions.name: Al Taawun and Al Khan
regions.note: Thirty minutes or more west on the coast. Families there send children into this belt, so the cluster's evening availability is set by the longest commute in it rather than the shortest.

sections.heading: Four University City households, and what each one underrates
paragraphs: The households in this district are easy to characterise and easy to mis-serve, because their strengths and blind spots are both unusual. Each of the four below asks a sophisticated question and tends to miss a simpler one.

The first is the academic household: one or both parents working on a campus, often in a discipline related to the child's weakest subject. They underrate how badly teaching your own teenager goes, and they overrate how much their own subject knowledge transfers to an examiner's mark scheme. The second is the postgraduate household, frequently on a fixed-term contract, whose child may change country mid-course. They underrate how little of an internal assessment transfers between schools.

The third is the destination-focused household, where a degree has been identified early and everything is being arranged around it. They underrate the risk of concentration: three Higher Level subjects all serving one plan, with no second route if the grade or the interest changes. The fourth is the local-supply household, making good use of affordable university-student tutors, who underrate the moment at which a Higher Level subject needs a specialist instead.

The table sets out what each household typically asks for and the question that would serve them better. None of these are criticisms; they are the predictable blind spots of people who are more informed than average and therefore more likely to be confident about the wrong variable. Being well informed in general is not the same as being current on one institution's entry text for one programme in one academic year, and that gap is where plans go wrong here.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation
paragraphs: This is the decision University City parents most often arrive with, and it deserves a careful answer rather than a slogan. The two Diploma mathematics courses are not a harder and an easier version of the same thing. They are different courses with different content, different assessment profiles and different downstream assumptions.

Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic and calculus-led route. At Higher Level it includes proof, complex numbers and advanced calculus, and it carries an unseen extended problem-solving paper. Applications and Interpretation is calculator-permitted throughout, with statistics and modelling carrying the weight, and its marks turn on interpreting a result in the context of the situation described rather than on manipulation.

The widespread claim that Applications and Interpretation is the soft option is misleading. It is a different difficulty, not a lesser one, and candidates who switch into it expecting relief often find the interpretation demands unfamiliar. The real question is not which is harder but which one the intended destination assumes, and that is answered on an admissions page rather than in a staff room.

What a family should do, concretely, is read the prerequisite text for two or three target programmes before the selection meeting, note whether each names a specific course or simply a level, and keep a second destination in view. Then choose with evidence. A tutor's useful role is assessing whether the candidate can carry Higher Level in either course, which is a different assessment from predicting a grade.

sections.heading: Where to read an admissions requirement, and where not to
paragraphs: Families in this district are unusually well connected to higher education and therefore unusually exposed to secondhand information about it. A colleague's recollection of what a faculty wanted three years ago is not a requirement, and the cost of acting on it is a closed route.

The rule is simple. For any institution, read the requirement on that institution's own admissions pages, note the academic year it applies to, and keep a copy. Where a programme states a specific subject at a specific level, treat it as binding. Where it states a general level without naming a course, write and ask. Admissions offices answer that question routinely and their answer is the only one that counts.

Equivalency sits alongside this and is separate from it. Recognition of a school-leaving certificate for use in the UAE is a Ministry of Education process, with its own published requirements, and it is not the same thing as meeting a university's entry standard. A family can satisfy one and not the other, which is why both need checking rather than one being assumed to imply the other.

Two things no page should do: publish a points threshold for the International Baccalaureate as an equivalency requirement without a source on moe.gov.ae, and imply that tutoring is required for equivalency, admission or progression. Neither is true, and the second is a manufactured urgency that an informed household will see through immediately.

Keep a file. Printed or saved admissions pages with the date they were read, the school's post-16 course guide, and any written answer from an admissions office are the three documents that settle arguments two years later. Requirements change between academic years, and the version that applies is the one current when the application is made, so the file is a record of what was reasonable to plan on rather than a guarantee.

sections.heading: Equivalency as a process, not a hurdle to be tutored over
paragraphs: Equivalency recognition is where the certificate a child earns becomes usable in the UAE, and in a district full of people who have been through foreign-credential processes it tends to be understood better than elsewhere. It is still worth setting out, because the published numbers are specific and one ranking competitor publishes them wrongly.

For the British track, guidance reported in July 2026 asks for five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among those five, plus either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Five is the number in the guidance; a competing page stating six is incorrect.

For the American track, the same guidance sets English proficiency at an IELTS academic score of 5, a TOEFL iBT score of 61, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics at a minimum of 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. No International Baccalaureate points figure appears in that guidance, so any page quoting one is quoting something unverified.

Three honest statements follow. The process is performed by the Ministry and by the emirate attestation channel, not by a school and certainly not by a tutoring platform. Nothing a tutor does accelerates or guarantees it. And subject choices made in Year 10 can affect whether the five-subject count is satisfied at all, which is the one place where tutoring and equivalency genuinely touch.

sections.heading: Why a parent with a doctorate should still hire a tutor
paragraphs: This section exists because the objection is reasonable and specific to this district. If a parent holds a research degree in physics, why pay someone else to teach IGCSE physics to their own child? The answer has three parts and none of them is about knowledge.

The first is the mark scheme. Examination marks are awarded against a published scheme with specific requirements about command verbs, naming, direction and linkage. A specialist knows the physics far better than the scheme requires and will frequently accept an answer that an examiner would not, because the answer is correct in substance and incomplete in form. Knowing what a question is worth is a separate skill from knowing the subject.

The second is the relationship. Teaching a fifteen-year-old requires the pupil to admit confusion repeatedly, and most adolescents will not do that in front of a parent. The sessions that result are short, defensive and unproductive, and they damage something that matters more than a grade. Families who have tried this generally do not need persuading.

The third is scheduling discipline. A paid external appointment happens. A parental promise to go through the paper on Saturday does not survive a busy fortnight. That is not a character flaw; it is how households work. The sensible division in an academic home is that the parent provides explanation and encouragement, and an external tutor provides marking, structure and an inescapable weekly deadline.

There is a version of this that works well, and it is worth naming. The parent reads the marked script after the session, understands exactly where the marks went, and reinforces that one point during the week without running a lesson. The subject knowledge in the house becomes useful again, applied to a diagnosis somebody else produced. That arrangement uses the household's real advantage without putting a parent in the one role an adolescent will not accept them in.

sections.heading: The university-student tutor question, answered properly
paragraphs: In a district built around campuses, the most available tutor is a university student, and the question of whether that is a good idea deserves a straight answer rather than a commercial one.

Legally the position is clear. The UAE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years, lists university students among its eligible applicants, alongside registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals and school students aged 15 to 18. A university student tutoring with that permit is doing something entirely proper, and tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws.

Practically, the fit depends on the level. For primary numeracy, lower secondary maths and science, and homework supervision, a capable undergraduate in the subject is often excellent value and brings recent experience of the material. Market rates for budget online tutoring run from the mid-double digits in AED per hour, well below specialist bands. For Higher Level Diploma subjects, internal assessment criteria and route advice, the requirement changes: those need somebody who has taught the level repeatedly and knows how it is marked.

The useful test is not the tutor's institution but their answer to two questions. Which board and level have you taught, and how many times? And what does criterion C ask for in this subject? A tutor who answers both specifically is worth hiring at any stage. One who cannot is worth hiring for homework supervision and not for a Higher Level grade.

sections.heading: Keeping a second route open
paragraphs: The characteristic risk in a destination-focused household is concentration. A plan is formed early, subjects are chosen to serve it, and by Year 13 there is no second door. That matters because two of the three variables in the plan are outside the family's control: the grade, and the student's continuing interest in the field.

A second route costs very little to maintain if it is planned at selection time. Often it means choosing one Higher Level subject that serves two fields rather than three that serve one, or keeping a numerate subject in the set, or choosing an Extended Essay question that reads credibly to two different faculties. These are design choices, not compromises, and they are nearly free if made in Year 11.

The conversation to have, once a year, is short. Name the first destination, name a plausible second, and check that the current subject set does not exclude the second. If it does, decide deliberately whether to accept that rather than discovering it at application time. Write the answer down, because the plan will drift and the written version is what makes the drift visible.

What tutoring contributes here is an honest read on capability rather than ambition. A candidate who is struggling at Standard Level in the subject their plan depends on at Higher Level needs to hear that in Year 11, when options exist. That assessment is uncomfortable, cheap and considerably more valuable than another term of weekly lessons.

sections.heading: Getting started when there is a destination in mind
paragraphs: The starting sequence for a route-driven household differs from the general one, because the first question is about options rather than about marks.

Begin by writing down the intended field and a second plausible one, then collect the prerequisite text for two or three programmes from the institutions' own pages with the academic year noted. Bring those to the first conversation along with the subject list, board, codes, tiers and levels, and the latest report. That set of documents turns a vague worry into a specific decision.

Then buy the cheapest useful hour, which is an assessment of whether the candidate can carry Higher Level in the route-critical subject. That is a different question from what grade they will get, and it is answerable from marked work under timed conditions. Only after that does weekly teaching make sense, and then in the subject the route actually depends on rather than across the whole set.

Finally, ask the uncomfortable questions early. Whether the specialist you need is free at your hour. What happens to an internal assessment if the family relocates mid-course. Whether anybody will tell you if the plan is not realistic. A provider that answers those three directly is one worth working with for two years, and in this district two years is usually what is being planned.

Set the review for once a term and keep it short. Has the marked work moved, is the subject set still consistent with both destinations, and has anything changed in the published prerequisites. Three questions, ten minutes, with the written note from last term in front of you. That is a lighter commitment than it sounds and it catches the two things that quietly ruin long plans: drift in the subject set, and a requirement that changed while nobody was reading.

process.title: Write down two destinations, not one
process.description: Name the intended field and a plausible second, then check the current subject set keeps both available. Doing this at selection time in Year 11 costs nothing; discovering a closed route at application time costs a year.

process.title: Collect the prerequisite text yourself
process.description: Read entry requirements on each institution's own admissions pages, note the academic year, and keep a copy. Where the text is ambiguous about a specific maths course or level, write to the admissions office and get the answer in writing.

process.title: Bring codes, tiers and levels
process.description: Board, syllabus or specification code, tier and level for every subject, plus the latest report. In a route conversation these determine which doors are still open, and a tier fixed at an entry deadline cannot be reopened afterwards.

process.title: Buy a capability assessment first
process.description: One hour of marked timed work in the route-critical subject answers whether the candidate can carry it at Higher Level. That is a more useful purchase than a term of weekly lessons chosen before anyone knows the answer.

process.title: Review the plan once a year, in writing
process.description: Re-check that the subject set still serves both destinations, and write down the conclusion. Plans drift quietly, and a written version from twelve months earlier is the only thing that makes the drift visible in time to act.

whyPoints.title: Routes treated as decisions with deadlines
whyPoints.description: Subject selection at the end of Year 11 and tier entry in Year 10 are the moments that open or close a destination. Sessions are positioned before those deadlines rather than after them, because afterwards the conversation is only about grades.

whyPoints.title: Requirements read, never remembered
whyPoints.description: Prerequisites come from the institution's own admissions pages with the academic year noted. No page, including this one, should tell you what a named faculty requires; it should tell you where to read it and what to ask if the text is ambiguous.

whyPoints.title: Equivalency described, not performed
whyPoints.description: The published British-track and American-track requirements are set out with their source and date. The process belongs to the Ministry and the attestation channel, no tutoring provider performs or accelerates it, and no unsourced IB points figure appears here.

whyPoints.title: Honest about who needs a specialist
whyPoints.description: A capable undergraduate is good value for primary and lower secondary work and the wrong choice for a Higher Level grade. Saying so costs a sale and saves a year, which in a district this well informed is the only position worth holding.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated plainly
whyPoints.description: IB Gram does not visit homes anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is an India-only service. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, and no regulator or examination board has approved, accredited or licensed IB Gram, which holds no such status.

whyPoints.title: The student's work stays their own
whyPoints.description: Tutors interrogate research questions, explain criteria and respond to drafts the student has written. No supplied text, no supplied data, no completed coursework, because a malpractice finding ends a diploma and no grade is worth that.

faqs.question: Which Diploma maths course should a University City student choose?
faqs.answer: Whichever one the intended destination assumes, which is a question for the programme's own admissions page rather than for a tutoring site. Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic and calculus-led route with restricted calculator use and an unseen problem-solving paper at Higher Level. Applications and Interpretation is calculator-permitted throughout with statistics, modelling and interpretation carrying the marks. Neither is the easy option; they are different courses. Read the prerequisite text for two or three target programmes before the Year 11 selection meeting.

faqs.question: Is Applications and Interpretation really the easier maths course?
faqs.answer: No, and students who switch expecting relief often regret it. The content is different rather than lighter: statistics, modelling and inference, with marks turning on interpreting a result in the context of the situation described. A candidate who can manipulate algebra fluently may find the interpretation demands unfamiliar and lose marks for correct answers with no stated meaning. The useful question is not which course is harder but which one keeps the intended degree available, and that is answered by the institution.

faqs.question: How do I find out what a university actually requires from an IB candidate?
faqs.answer: Read it on that institution's own admissions pages, note which academic year the requirement applies to, and keep a copy. Where a programme names a specific subject at a specific level, treat that as binding. Where it states a level without naming a course, write to the admissions office and ask for confirmation in writing, which they answer routinely. A colleague's recollection of a requirement from three years ago is the least reliable source available and the most commonly used.

faqs.question: Does meeting the Ministry's equivalency rules mean a university will accept my child?
faqs.answer: No. They are separate processes with separate standards. Equivalency is recognition of a school-leaving certificate for use in the UAE, administered by the Ministry of Education with the emirate attestation channel, and its published thresholds are a floor rather than a competitive entry standard. A university sets its own entry requirements, often considerably higher. A family can satisfy one and not the other, so both need checking independently rather than assuming either implies the other.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does the Ministry count for the British track?
faqs.answer: Five. The guidance reported in July 2026 asks for five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not included among those five, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. One competing page in this market states six, which is wrong. Verify the current rule on moe.gov.ae before making a subject decision on the basis of it.

faqs.question: Can anyone tell me the Diploma points total the Ministry asks for?
faqs.answer: Not in the guidance available. The July 2026 reporting that sets out the British and American track requirements states no International Baccalaureate points threshold, so any page quoting one is quoting something unverified. If you need that figure, read it on moe.gov.ae or ask the emirate attestation authority directly and keep their answer. A tutoring provider publishing a specific IB points number without that source is guessing with your child's application.

faqs.question: My child's school may not let them take Higher Level maths. Can that be challenged?
faqs.answer: It can be informed, which works better than challenging it. Sixth-form prerequisites are set by the school and usually rest on IGCSE tier and grade. The persuasive move is evidence: have the candidate sit Higher Level style material or Extended tier past papers under timed conditions, marked strictly, and take the mark to the head of department. A parent's conviction rarely moves a decision; a marked script from an independent source sometimes does. Raise it before the selection meeting, not after.

faqs.question: I teach this subject myself. Why would I pay someone else?
faqs.answer: Three reasons, none about knowledge. Mark schemes award marks for command verbs, naming and linkage, and a specialist routinely accepts answers an examiner would not because they are correct in substance and incomplete in form. Teenagers will rarely admit confusion repeatedly in front of a parent, which makes parent-taught sessions short and defensive. And a paid external appointment happens, while a promise to go through the paper on Saturday does not survive a busy fortnight. Keep the explaining; outsource the marking.

faqs.question: Are university students allowed to work as private tutors in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Yes, with a permit. The private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 is granted free of charge for two years and lists university students among eligible applicants, alongside registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals and school students aged 15 to 18. Tutoring without the permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published. Asking a prospective tutor to show the permit is entirely reasonable.

faqs.question: Is a student tutor from a nearby campus good enough for Higher Level work?
faqs.answer: For primary numeracy, lower secondary maths and science and homework supervision, often yes, and at market budget rates of roughly AED 33 to 150 an hour it is good value. For Higher Level Diploma subjects, internal assessment criteria and route advice, the requirement changes to someone who has taught that level repeatedly. Two questions sort it quickly: which board and level have you taught and how often, and what does a named criterion in this subject actually ask for. Specific answers to both are the signal.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send tutors to homes near the campuses?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not make home visits anywhere in the UAE, and in-home tutoring is a service run only in India. Lessons for University City families are delivered one-to-one over live video. In a district with a genuine local tutor supply this is a deliberate trade: the choice of tutor is made on subject, level and route knowledge rather than on who lives within a short walk, which matters most precisely where the local pool is thinnest.

faqs.question: What happens to an internal assessment if we relocate mid-Diploma?
faqs.answer: Less transfers than families expect, and this is the question postgraduate households should ask first. Internal assessment work is submitted through a school, against that school's internal deadlines and with its supervision records, so a mid-course move can mean restarting a component or negotiating its transfer. Ask both schools what their process is before the move rather than after, and ask the receiving school's coordinator specifically about supervision records. A tutor can help rebuild the work; they cannot move the administration.

faqs.question: Should all three Higher Level subjects serve the same intended degree?
faqs.answer: Usually not, because it leaves no second route if the grade or the interest changes. A cheaper design is one Higher Level subject that serves two fields, a numerate subject kept in the set, and an Extended Essay question that reads credibly to two different faculties. These choices cost almost nothing at the Year 11 selection meeting and are nearly impossible to retrofit in Year 13. Decide deliberately rather than by default, and write the decision down.

faqs.question: How early should route conversations start?
faqs.answer: At the beginning of Year 10, which is earlier than most schools raise it. Tier entries for Cambridge subjects are fixed at an entry deadline months before the papers, and dropping a subject to lighten a Year 10 timetable can close a Higher Level door two years later. By the end of Year 11 the subject set is largely settled. A single hour spent on prerequisites and tier implications at the start of Year 10 is the highest-value planning any family here can buy.

faqs.question: Will a tutor tell us if the plan is not realistic?
faqs.answer: That is the question to ask before hiring one, and the answer should be yes. A candidate struggling at Standard Level in the subject their plan depends on at Higher Level needs to hear that in Year 11, when alternatives exist, rather than in Year 13. An honest read on capability comes from marked work under timed conditions rather than from impressions, and it is a different judgement from predicting a final grade. No provider should offer a grade guarantee, and anyone who does is telling you something.

sharjah/university-city.closingHeading: Decide the route before you buy the lessons
sharjah/university-city.closingBody: Households in University City are generally well informed and short of one thing: the prerequisite text for the programmes they are aiming at, read from the source and written down. Collect that, bring the subject list with codes, tiers and levels, and the first hour can go on whether the candidate can carry the route-critical subject at Higher Level. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, equivalency figures here carry their source and date, and the student writes every word of their own assessed work.

intro.heading: The regulator behind your child's school decides what you can check
paragraphs: Private schools in Umm Al Quwain are licensed and inspected by the federal Ministry of Education, not by KHDA and not by ADEK. A parent in Dubai can open a KHDA report for a named school, read a six-band judgement, see the evidence behind it and compare it with last year's. A parent in Al Salamah or Al Raas is working with less published paper, and the school's own prospectus fills the gap. That changes how you choose tutoring support, because the first question — is my child behind the school, or behind the syllabus? — is harder to answer from documents.

The second fact that shapes this page is distance. Most internationally-schooled students here commute out of the emirate: to Muwaileh and University City in Sharjah, to Ajman, or north to Al Hamra in Ras Al Khaimah. A child who leaves Al Riqqa at 6:40am and is home at 4pm has a narrow evening left. An in-home arrangement in that window means a tutor driving the same roads in the same traffic your child just sat in, and the session time moves whenever the road does.

So IB Gram teaches Umm Al Quwain students one-to-one over live video. Nobody is sent to an address in this emirate — home visits are a service we run only in India, and that is stated on every country page on this site. What a UAQ family gets instead is the whole specialist pool rather than the fraction of it inside a 30-minute drive: a Chemistry HL teacher who marks scientific investigations against the current guide, or an Edexcel 4MA1 Higher specialist, holding a 7pm slot that does not shift because the E311 is slow.

This page is written around that regulatory gap. It sets out which authority inspects what across the seven emirates, what each of the six inspection bands actually describes, and the three questions a report will not answer about your own child. Then the practical layer: market tutoring rates in AED with the providers who charge them named, the evening window after each commute, the exam calendar counted backwards from a May session, MoE equivalency before a UAE university application, and the criterion letters an Internal Assessment is marked against.

Two things are off the table here. A tutor does not write, draft or edit an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay or a TOK essay; the IB treats that as malpractice, and the provider selling finished coursework is selling your child a withdrawn diploma. And nobody on this platform predicts a grade. What a specialist does is read the mark scheme with your child, work out which criterion or which paper is losing the marks, and make them practise the thing that moves it.

umm-al-quwain.programmesIntro: Four programmes cover almost every Umm Al Quwain student who needs subject support. Which one your child sits depends on the school they commute to rather than on the emirate you live in, and the two IGCSE boards behind the same subject name are chosen by that school. Each note below says what the programme looks like from a UAQ address specifically.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP runs on criterion-based assessment: four criteria per subject, each marked out of 8, converted into a 1-7 grade using boundaries the school applies. There are no external papers until the optional Year 11 eAssessment. For a parent that means a report-card grade is a professional judgement against published descriptors, and the useful question is which criterion the marks are coming off — knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, or reflecting.
programmes.countryNote: UAQ students in MYP are usually in a Sharjah or Ajman school where the cohort is small and sets are mixed. The real risk is the step into the Diploma: a student scoring 6s on criterion A can still meet Maths AA HL algebra cold. A MYP tutor in Umm Al Quwain earns their keep in Years 9 and 10, before subject and level choices are locked.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The Diploma is six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS. It is marked out of 45: seven points per subject, up to three bonus points from the EE and TOK matrix, and 24 points to pass with no failing conditions. Internal Assessment carries 20% in most subjects, so a fifth of the grade is settled months before the exam hall opens.
programmes.countryNote: Only a handful of schools within reach of Umm Al Quwain run the full Diploma, so subject choice is constrained by which timetable blocks collide rather than by preference. An IB Diploma tutor in Umm Al Quwain is often covering a Higher Level the school teaches in a combined class, HL and SL in one room, which is where the HL-only content quietly goes missing.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Cambridge IGCSE is examined subject by subject against a syllabus code you can look up: 0580 Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry, 0610 Biology, 0455 Economics. Most subjects split into Core and Extended, and the tier sets the grade ceiling — Core cannot reach the top grades at all. Sciences are assessed by written papers, including an alternative-to-practical paper, rather than by coursework.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge is the common board in the Sharjah and Ajman schools UAQ families use, and the October/November series matters here: a student who moved mid-year from an Indian or ministry-curriculum school often ends up on a split series. A Cambridge IGCSE tutor in Umm Al Quwain should be told the series and the tier before the first lesson, because both change the paper set.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE uses its own codes — 4MA1 Mathematics A, 4PH1 Physics, 4CH1 Chemistry, 4BI1 Biology — and tiers mathematics into Foundation and Higher. It runs a January series as well as May/June, which Cambridge does not, so a resit can happen within months rather than after a full year. Papers are structured differently from Cambridge's even where the content overlaps almost completely.
programmes.countryNote: A UAQ student retaking Mathematics A 4MA1 in January is a common northern-emirates case: the June grade arrives in August, a sixth-form or university condition is missed by one grade, and roughly fourteen teaching weeks remain. That is a scheduling problem as much as a teaching one, and a fixed online slot is what makes those fourteen weeks usable from this emirate.

umm-al-quwain.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects Umm Al Quwain families ask about most, with what each one actually assesses and where the marks go missing. Where a subject exists on both boards the syllabus code is given, because 0580 and 4MA1 are different papers with different question styles even though both say IGCSE Mathematics on the certificate.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: AA is the proof-and-calculus route. At HL, Paper 1 without a calculator is 30%, Paper 2 with one is 30%, Paper 3 extended response is 20% and the exploration is 20%. Paper 3 decides most HL grades: two long, unfamiliar, scaffolded investigations. The marks usually go missing in reasoning the student had in their head and never wrote down.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: AI is the modelling-and-statistics route, built around the graphing calculator. The common error is treating it as the soft option: AI HL statistics, with chi-squared, regression and hypothesis testing, is heavier than anything in AA SL, and the exploration still carries 20%. Several engineering programmes will not accept AI HL in place of AA HL.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Internal Assessment is 20% and the written papers carry the remaining 80%. Under the current guide the scientific investigation is marked out of 24 across research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation. Marks disappear in uncertainty handling, and in a closing paragraph that describes the graph instead of testing the hypothesis against accepted values.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics are where Higher Level students stall, and the HL-only extensions are the first thing a combined HL/SL class skips. The investigation is 20% and needs a measurable variable, enough trials to support a real uncertainty, and a conclusion tied to literature values. Cambridge IGCSE 0620 feeds straight into this course.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Volume is the problem rather than difficulty. Command terms decide the marks: outline is not explain, and suggest wants a principle applied to an unseen context. Data-based questions on an unfamiliar experiment reward practice, not rereading. Students arriving from IGCSE 0610 already have much of the vocabulary and underestimate the step in depth.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: The portfolio of three commentaries, 800 words each, is 30% of the SL grade and 20% at HL, and it is marked on diagram use and real-world linkage far more than on the article chosen. HL adds quantitative work and policy analysis. Most lost marks sit in diagrams that are drawn neatly and then never referred to in the text.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The research project is written against a real organisation and a real question, which is where a UAQ student with a family business has an advantage over a classmate guessing at one. Tool application — Ansoff, BCG, break-even — only earns marks when the output changes the recommendation. Case-study papers reward structure: context, tool, judgement.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Paper 1 is an unseen guided analysis of a non-literary text and Paper 2 a comparative essay on studied works. The Individual Oral is 20% at HL and 30% at SL, and HL adds an essay of 1,200 to 1,500 words. The learner portfolio is not assessed, yet the oral depends entirely on how seriously it was kept.

subjects.name: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics (0580)
subjects.description: Extended is the tier that keeps the top grades open and the one nearly every Diploma-bound student needs. It sits Papers 2 and 4, each worth half the grade. Marks go to method rather than arithmetic: unrounded intermediate values carried through a calculation, missing units, and working an examiner cannot follow to the answer.

subjects.name: Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A (4MA1)
subjects.description: Two papers, each 50%, both with a calculator. Higher tier reports on the 9-1 scale with the grade 9 questions concentrated at the back of each paper. The January series makes 4MA1 the practical retake route for a student who missed a sixth-form or foundation-year condition in August by a single grade.

regions.note: The newer waterfront development on the Al Salamah side, with a younger expatriate intake and a lot of Sharjah and Ajman enrolment. UAQ Marina online tuition slots mostly start at 6:30pm or later, after the bus run and before a late family dinner.

regions.name: Al Salamah
regions.note: The main residential spread south of the lagoon, closest to the Ajman border and the shortest run in the emirate to a Sharjah school gate. A 5:30pm start is realistic here on most weekdays, which is the earliest usable window anywhere in UAQ.

regions.name: Al Raas
regions.note: Al Raas 1, 2 and 3 sit on the older side of town near the corniche. Villa households here often have two or three siblings on different boards, so the practical booking is two subjects in one evening rather than one subject twice a week.

regions.name: Al Riqqa
regions.note: Inland and close to the E311 interchange, which is both the advantage and the problem: fast out at 6:30am, slow back at 4pm. Families here tend to take the 7pm or 8pm slot and hold it fixed for the whole term rather than moving it weekly.

regions.name: Al Haditha and the old town
regions.note: The historic quarter on the peninsula beside Khor Al Beidah, home to the emirate's oldest schools and a largely Emirati intake. The common request here is Arabic and Islamic Studies support running alongside an IGCSE timetable, not instead of it.

regions.name: Al Humrah
regions.note: South-east of the centre towards the Sharjah boundary, mixed villa and staff accommodation. Students here are more often in Ajman schools, so a 6pm start works, and the half-hour saved against a Sharjah commute is worth building the timetable around.

regions.name: Falaj Al Mualla
regions.note: The inland UAQ exclave, roughly 50km from the coast and agricultural. There is effectively no local specialist pool at all, which makes this the clearest case in the emirate for one-to-one online: the alternative is an hour of driving each way before anyone opens a book.

regions.name: Al Salam City
regions.note: A newer development on the Ajman side with a fast-growing young population. Demand here is mostly MYP and IGCSE rather than Diploma, and families book earlier slots because the school run is short enough to leave the evening intact.

sections.heading: Why the Ministry of Education, not KHDA, inspects your child's school
paragraphs: Umm Al Quwain has no emirate-level schools authority of its own. Private schools here are licensed and inspected by the federal Ministry of Education, as they are in Ajman, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah. Dubai has KHDA, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain have ADEK, Sharjah has SPEA. Four of the seven emirates sit with the ministry and Umm Al Quwain is one of them. That is not a quality judgement in either direction; it is a difference in which body writes the rules and where the resulting paperwork ends up.

The practical consequence for a parent is the report. KHDA publishes a named report per Dubai school each inspection cycle, which is why a Dubai parent can read a judgement, see the evidence an inspector used and compare it against the previous year. A Ministry of Education inspection in Umm Al Quwain uses the same national six-band vocabulary — Outstanding, Very Good, Good, Acceptable, Weak, Very Weak — but the reports are not published on the same public schedule, and some schools have not been visited recently. Ask the school directly for its latest report and the date on it: a judgement three years old describes a staff body that may have turned over twice.

There is a second consequence that catches families moving north from Dubai or Sharjah. Fee regulation, inspection timing and the complaints route all sit with the regulator rather than with the school, so the process you used in Dubai does not transfer. If your child attends school in Sharjah while you live in Umm Al Quwain, which is the common pattern here, the school answers to SPEA and your emirate answers to the ministry. Knowing which door to knock on saves a term of forwarded emails.

sections.heading: What each inspection band says, and where tutoring actually fits
paragraphs: The six bands describe a school, not a student. An Outstanding school still has a bottom set in Maths AA HL, and a school rated Acceptable still produces 40-point Diplomas. The band is useful as a prior rather than as a diagnosis: it tells you how likely the school is to catch a problem early, and how likely the HL-only content is to be taught properly. It tells you nothing about whether your child can integrate by substitution.

Read the band alongside the thing it rarely covers, which is subject-level provision. A school can be Good overall and still teach HL and SL Chemistry in one room, and that single arrangement is the most common reason a UAQ Higher Level student arrives with gaps invisible on a report card. Ask which Higher Levels run as their own class, how many students are in each, and whether the teacher has taken a cohort through a May session before. Those three answers predict the need for support better than the overall judgement does.

Where the band does change the decision is in frequency and scope. In a strong school with separate HL classes, one weekly session on the weakest topic cluster is usually enough. Where a subject is taught in a combined class, or where the teacher changed mid-year, support has to cover delivery as well as practice, and that is a different brief and a different number of hours. Say which of the two situations you are in when you enquire, because it changes the match more than the subject name does.

sections.heading: The evening window after the Sharjah, Ajman and RAK school run
paragraphs: The hardest constraint on tutoring in this emirate is not money or supply. It is the clock. A child at a Muwaileh or University City school leaves home between 6:15 and 6:45am and is back between 3:30 and 4:30pm depending on the bus. Add a prayer, a meal and whatever activity runs after school, and the first genuinely productive start is 6pm, more often 6:30pm or 7pm. Evening tuition after the Sharjah school run has to fit that window, and anything booked into it has to be worth the slot.

This is where an in-home arrangement strains in Umm Al Quwain in a way it does not in Dubai. A tutor driving from Sharjah to Al Raas is repeating the trip your child has just finished, in the same direction, at the same hour. Either the travel is priced into the rate — the in-home market band of AED 180 to 500 an hour reported by Bestimate includes it — or the lesson starts late, or it starts earlier than a tired student can use. Online removes the variable: 7pm means 7pm, and a missed lesson is rescheduled rather than lost to a road.

The second timing fact is the week. UAE schools run Monday to Friday with the weekend on Saturday and Sunday, and the Friday finish is early. Friday afternoon and Sunday morning are the two slots families underuse, and they are the right ones for a long coursework session where a 50-minute weekday block is not enough. For a student sitting a May session, a standing 90-minute Sunday slot from January is worth more than two tired weekday halves.

sections.heading: What tutoring costs around Umm Al Quwain, in AED
paragraphs: Nobody in this market publishes a rate table for IGCSE tuition in Umm Al Quwain or anywhere else in the northern emirates, which is why parents end up comparing prices by phoning round. The figures below are market rates collected from published UAE tutoring sites and from Bestimate's 2026 Dubai tutoring cost survey. They are what other providers charge, not an IB Gram price list: our own rate is agreed after a consultation and a free trial lesson, because an hour of Maths AA HL coursework support and an hour of Year 7 maths are not the same product.

Three things move a quoted rate more than anything else. Format first: travel time sits inside an in-home rate, which is why the in-home band starts roughly AED 30 to 50 an hour above the online equivalent for the same qualification. Level second: IGCSE support sits below Diploma support, and Higher Level sciences and Maths AA HL sit at the top of the range. Timing third: rates firm up from February as May-session demand concentrates, so the same tutor is cheaper booked in January than in March.

Umm Al Quwain adds one local distortion. Few specialist subject teachers live in the emirate, so an in-home quote here is usually a Sharjah or Dubai tutor pricing a 40 to 70-minute drive into the hour. Online pricing carries none of that, which is why the gap between the two formats is wider in the northern emirates than it is in Dubai. Ask any provider what the number includes — travel, materials, marking, VAT — and whether it is per hour or per session, because those are the two places a quote stops matching the invoice.

sections.heading: An IB home tutor in Umm Al Quwain: what that search really gets you
paragraphs: The phrase parents type is IB home tutor in Umm Al Quwain, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a redirect. Private home tutoring in this emirate exists, it is legal, and the permit a private tutor needs is obtained through MoHRE and issued free of charge. What it is not is abundant. The number of people living within a short drive of Al Salamah who can teach Chemistry HL to the current guide, or mark an Economics portfolio against the right criteria, is very small.

So the real choice is not online against in-home. It is a nearby generalist against a subject specialist reached over video. For Year 7 maths homework the generalist is fine and convenience wins outright. For a Higher Level subject, a coursework deadline, or an IGCSE retake with a university condition attached, the specialist is the one who moves the mark, and in Umm Al Quwain that person is almost never ten minutes away. IB Gram teaches Umm Al Quwain students one-to-one over live video for that reason and does not send anyone to a UAQ address; home visits are a service we run only in India.

Two practical objections to online come up, and both are fair. Science practicals cannot happen over video: the tutor works on the write-up, the uncertainty treatment and the evaluation, while the practical itself happens at school, which is where it is assessed anyway. And a younger student does need an adult in earshot for the first few sessions. The format works from roughly Year 7 upward, and below that the limit is attention span, not technology.

sections.heading: The exam calendar, counted backwards from a May session
paragraphs: Competitor pages in this market do not mention exam sessions at all, which is odd, because the calendar decides whether tutoring arrives in time to matter. Work backwards instead. A Diploma candidate sitting a May session is registered by their school the previous autumn, with the school's own internal deadline falling weeks before that. By the time a parent sees a worrying January report card, the subjects and the levels are already fixed for that session.

The Internal Assessment deadlines land before that report card too. Most schools want final maths explorations and science investigations between October and January of the second Diploma year, and the Extended Essay final submission around the same window. A tutor brought in during February can still move exam technique and content, but the 20% already banked in the IA is banked. If your child is in the first Diploma year now, the highest-value eight weeks of tutoring in the whole programme are the ones around the IA draft.

IGCSE runs on a different clock. Cambridge's main series is May/June with results in mid-August, and the October/November series reports in mid-January. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE adds a January series reporting in early March, which is the practical retake route. Centre entry deadlines sit several months before each series, and an exam centre taking private candidates closes earlier still, so a retake decision taken after August results day is already a November or January decision rather than a June one.

sections.heading: MoE equivalency and attestation before a UAE university application
paragraphs: An IB Diploma, or a set of IGCSEs and A Levels, is not automatically usable for a UAE university place or a government job. The Ministry of Education issues an equivalency certificate, the mu'adala, that maps a foreign qualification onto the UAE system, and universities and employers ask to see it. Nobody in this tutoring market mentions it, and families in the northern emirates tend to meet it late, usually in the week an application is due.

MoE equivalency for IB students and for British-curriculum students follows the same broad route, and the shape of the requirement is stable even where the detail changes: a minimum number of subjects at or above a stated grade, with English and mathematics among them, a leaving certificate from a licensed school, and attestation of any document issued outside the UAE. For British-curriculum students that usually means a specified count of IGCSE passes plus AS or A Level passes; for Diploma students, the IB transcript and the diploma itself. Check the ministry's current published rules rather than assuming last year's still apply.

Two details matter particularly here. First, Arabic and, for Muslim students, Islamic Studies are ministry-mandated subjects in UAE private schools and are recorded on school documents, so a student who treated them as optional discovers it at exactly this point. Second, documents issued abroad — a transcript from a school in India or the UK — need attestation before the ministry will accept them, and that chain takes weeks rather than days. Start it in the autumn of the final year, not after results day.

sections.heading: Where IA marks go missing, criterion letter by criterion letter
paragraphs: Internal Assessment is the part of the Diploma a tutor can legitimately influence most, and the part schools give the least structured feedback on. It is also the part nobody writes about: no competitor page in this market names a single criterion. The marks are allocated publicly and by letter, which is why IA feedback for Umm Al Quwain students starts with the criterion letters rather than with the prose. A student who knows which letter is costing them can fix it in one session instead of rewriting from scratch.

The mathematics exploration is marked out of 20 across five criteria: presentation (4 marks), mathematical communication (4), personal engagement (3), reflection (3) and use of mathematics (6). The last two are where the marks sit and where they vanish. Reflection means evaluating the limitations of the model rather than restating the result, and use of mathematics at Higher Level means the mathematics has to be commensurate with the course, which an exploration built on GCSE-level trigonometry never is.

Science investigations are marked out of 24 under the current guide, across research design, data analysis, conclusion and evaluation at six marks each. Three patterns account for most of the losses: a research question with no measurable independent variable, data presented with no uncertainty treatment, and a conclusion that describes the graph instead of comparing it with accepted values. The Extended Essay is marked out of 34, and critical thinking alone carries 12 of those marks — more than presentation and engagement combined, which is the reverse of how most students spend their time.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not do with your child's coursework
paragraphs: There is a provider in this market advertising completed Internal Assessments at around AED 3,750. A student who submits one has committed malpractice under the IB's academic honesty regulations, and the sanction is the loss of the subject grade or of the whole diploma, applied after the fact. The risk is not hypothetical, and it is not the seller's risk: it lands entirely on the candidate, who also signs a declaration that the work submitted is their own.

The line the IB draws is about authorship, and it is workable in practice. A tutor may teach the underlying content, explain what a criterion is asking for, model a worked example on a different topic, question a research question until the student sharpens it, point at a paragraph that does not answer the criterion, and check a word count. A tutor may not supply sentences, restructure the argument on the page, write the analysis, generate the data or edit the draft. The school supervisor signs an authorship declaration as well.

The distinction shows up in how a session actually runs. A legitimate coursework session is mostly the student talking and typing while the tutor asks what the criterion wants and whether the paragraph delivers it. If your child leaves a session holding a better document they did not write, you have bought a liability rather than a grade. Ask any provider, including us, to state that boundary in writing before a coursework block starts: it is a reasonable question and the answer should take one line.
bullets: A tutor may explain a criterion, question a research question and name an unanswered one
