sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Studies and moral education beside an IB timetable
paragraphs: A UAQ family enquiring about tutoring usually asks about Maths HL or Chemistry, then mentions Arabic almost as an afterthought. It is not an afterthought. The Ministry of Education requires Arabic in licensed private schools, Islamic Studies for Muslim students, and a moral and social studies strand, and those subjects appear on school reports and in the documents an equivalency file needs. They also sit on the same weekly timetable as six Diploma subjects, the Extended Essay and CAS.

The usual problem is a student who joined the UAE system late. Arabic as an additional language from Year 7 is a different experience from Arabic from Year 1, and a Diploma year is a poor time to discover the gap. What matters most is not the grade itself but the hours it consumes: a student spending five hours a week catching up on Arabic has five hours less for Paper 3 practice, and a Diploma timetable has no spare hours built into it anywhere.

Two honest points about this. The first is that specialist support for these subjects is scarcer online than for maths or physics, and we will say so rather than match a student to someone who is not a specialist. The second is that the fix is often scheduling rather than teaching: moving Arabic revision into the Friday afternoon or Sunday morning slot protects the weekday evenings for subjects carrying Higher Level papers. Say at the enquiry stage if Arabic or Islamic Studies is part of the picture, because it reshapes the whole timetable.

process.title: Tell us the school, the board and the paper
process.description: An enquiry that says Year 11, Cambridge IGCSE Physics 0625, Extended tier, Muwaileh school, grade 6 in the mock, losing marks on electricity gets matched within a day. One that says needs physics help takes a week of emails. Include the commute, because it decides which evening slots are real rather than theoretical.

process.title: A diagnostic hour on the real paper
process.description: The first session is not teaching. A tutor works through a past paper or a marked script with your child and reports back on where the marks are going: topic knowledge, technique, or misreading the command term. That report becomes the brief for everything after it, and it is worth having even if you stop there.

process.title: Match to a syllabus specialist, then trial
process.description: We match on the syllabus code and the paper rather than on proximity, and the free trial lesson exists so your child can reject the match. A tutor who is strong on 0580 Extended is not automatically the right IB Maths AA HL tutor online. If the fit is wrong, say so after the trial and we match again.

process.title: Fix the slot around the commute
process.description: The timetable is set once and then kept: a named evening, a named time in Gulf Standard Time, and a plan for Ramadan and exam weeks agreed in advance. Because lessons are one-to-one and online, the slot does not move when the road does. Reschedules are handled week by week rather than by losing the hour.

process.title: Review every six weeks against the school's calendar
process.description: Progress is checked against your child's own assessments — the next school test, the IA draft deadline, the mock — rather than against a generic scheme of work. If six weeks produce nothing, that is information: either the brief was wrong or the match is, and both are fixable without starting the search again.

whyPoints.title: We read the regulator, not just the report card
whyPoints.description: A Ministry of Education emirate publishes less about its schools than Dubai does, so we ask the questions a report would have answered: whether the Higher Level runs as its own class, how many students are in it, and whether the teacher has taken a cohort through a May session. Those answers shape the brief.

whyPoints.title: Matched by syllabus code, not by postcode
whyPoints.description: 0580 and 4MA1 are different papers. AA HL and AI HL are different courses. A tutor is matched to the exact syllabus, tier and paper your child sits, which is the whole point of teaching online from an emirate where the resident specialist pool is thin.

whyPoints.title: Honest about availability
whyPoints.description: Where no specialist is free for a subject — some of the less common Diploma languages, Arabic at Diploma level, a few Higher Level options — we say so and say when, instead of filling the slot with a generalist. A wrong match costs a term, and a term in a Diploma year is expensive.

whyPoints.title: The coursework boundary is in writing
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches the criteria, questions the research question and marks against the published descriptors. Nobody drafts, edits or supplies text for an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay or a TOK essay, and we will confirm that in writing before a coursework block begins.

whyPoints.title: Scheduled for this emirate's evening, not Dubai's
whyPoints.description: Sessions are built around the Sharjah, Ajman and Ras Al Khaimah school run, with Friday afternoon and Sunday morning kept for long coursework work. Ramadan timing is agreed before the month starts rather than improvised in its first week.

whyPoints.title: No predictions about grades
whyPoints.description: Nobody on this platform predicts a score. What a specialist offers is a diagnosis against the mark scheme, practice on the papers your child will actually sit, and a written record of what changed between reviews. Treat any provider who offers a number instead with real scepticism.

faqs.question: Which authority inspects private schools in Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: The federal Ministry of Education. Umm Al Quwain has no emirate-level schools regulator of its own, unlike Dubai with KHDA, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain with ADEK, and Sharjah with SPEA. Ministry inspections in the northern emirates use the same national six-band vocabulary — Outstanding, Very Good, Good, Acceptable, Weak, Very Weak — but reports are not published on the same annual public schedule as Dubai's. Ask the school directly for its most recent inspection outcome and check the date on it, because a judgement three years old describes a staff body that may have turned over twice since the inspectors left.

faqs.question: How much does a private tutor cost per hour in Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: These are market rates across the UAE rather than ours. Budget online tutoring advertises from about AED 45 to 150 an hour, a qualified subject tutor online runs roughly AED 150 to 300, an in-home visit with travel inside the rate sits around AED 180 to 500, and IB or IGCSE specialists are quoted between AED 200 and 450 or above. Those figures come from published provider pages and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai survey. In Umm Al Quwain the in-home end tends to sit higher because a quote usually prices in a drive from Sharjah or Dubai. Our own rate is agreed after a consultation and a free trial.

faqs.question: Can I get an IB home tutor in Umm Al Quwain, or is tuition online only?
faqs.answer: Private home tutoring exists in the emirate and is legal with a permit, but the local pool of Diploma-level subject specialists is very small, so most in-home quotes come from a tutor driving up from Sharjah or Dubai with travel priced in. IB Gram teaches Umm Al Quwain students one-to-one over live video and does not send anyone to a UAQ address; home visits are a service we run only in India. The trade is deliberate. You get a Chemistry HL or Maths AA HL specialist in a fixed 7pm slot instead of whoever happens to live within a 30-minute drive.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in Umm Al Quwain need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a permit obtained through MoHRE, and every official source checked states that the permit itself is issued free of charge. Anyone charging for tutoring without one is working outside the rules, and a resident in employment also needs their employer's agreement before applying. The ministry has said it will act against unlicensed tutoring but has not published penalty amounts, so treat any specific figure circulating online as unverified. If you hire an individual privately, ask to see the permit; if you use a platform, ask how it checks the people it sends you.

faqs.question: My child commutes to a school in Sharjah, so when can a session realistically start?
faqs.answer: Plan on 6:30pm. A child at a Muwaileh or University City school leaves Umm Al Quwain between 6:15 and 6:45am and is usually home between 3:30 and 4:30pm, and after a meal and a break the first productive hour begins at about 6:30. From Ajman schools a 5:30pm or 6pm start works; from Ras Al Khaimah, nearer 7pm. Those are weekday-evening estimates rather than a timetable. One advantage of online sessions is that the start time holds whatever the E311 is doing, which no in-home arrangement in this emirate can offer.

faqs.question: Is online tutoring as effective as in-person for a student in Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: For one-to-one subject teaching from about Year 7 upward, the match matters more than the format. A shared screen, a digital whiteboard and the student's own marked script cover nearly everything a desk does, and notes after each session let a parent see what happened. Two honest limits: a younger child needs an adult in earshot for the first few sessions, and science practicals stay at school where they are assessed, with the tutor working on the write-up, the uncertainties and the evaluation. In an emirate with few resident specialists, the alternative is usually a generalist rather than a better teacher.

faqs.question: Does my child need MoE equivalency to apply to a UAE university from Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: For most UAE universities, and for government employment, yes. The Ministry of Education issues an equivalency certificate that maps an IB Diploma or a British-curriculum certificate set onto the UAE system. The file usually wants the certificates themselves, a school leaving certificate, and attestation of anything issued outside the country. Requirements change, so check the ministry's current rules rather than a forum post. The part that catches northern-emirates families is the attestation chain for documents from a previous school abroad, which takes weeks. Start in the autumn of the final year rather than after results day.

faqs.question: Are Arabic and Islamic Studies compulsory alongside IB and IGCSE here?
faqs.answer: The Ministry of Education requires Arabic in licensed private schools, Islamic Studies for Muslim students, and a moral and social studies strand, and these sit on the timetable alongside IB or IGCSE subjects. They also appear on the school documents an equivalency file needs, which is where a student who treated them as optional runs into difficulty. The practical cost is time rather than difficulty: hours spent catching up on Arabic are hours not spent on a Higher Level paper. Specialist online support for these subjects is scarcer than for maths or physics, and we say so when none is available.

faqs.question: Can a tutor write or correct my child's IB Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: No. A tutor may teach the content, explain what each criterion asks for, work an example on a different topic, question the research question until the student sharpens it, point at a paragraph that misses a criterion, and check a word count. A tutor may not supply sentences, restructure the argument on the page, generate data or edit the draft. The candidate signs an authorship declaration and so does the school supervisor. One provider in this market advertises completed Internal Assessments at around AED 3,750; a student who submits one risks losing the subject grade or the diploma itself.

faqs.question: When does my child's school register them for IB exams?
faqs.answer: Schools submit candidate registrations to the IB in the autumn for a May session and in the spring for a November session, and each school sets its own internal deadline weeks earlier again. By the time a January report card raises an alarm, the subjects and levels for May are fixed. The same logic applies to IGCSE: centre entry deadlines sit several months before each series, and an exam centre taking private candidates closes earlier still. If a tier or series decision is in play, Core against Extended or June against a January retake, have that conversation in the autumn term.

faqs.question: Which IB maths route should my child take, Analysis and Approaches or Applications?
faqs.answer: AA is the algebra, proof and calculus route; AI is modelling and statistics built around the graphing calculator. AI is not the soft option, since AI HL statistics is heavier than anything in AA SL, but the choice should follow the intended degree rather than comfort. Engineering, physics, mathematics, computer science and most quantitative economics programmes expect Higher Level maths and often specify AA, and some will not accept AI HL in its place. Check the exact programme pages at the universities your child is aiming at, including Khalifa University, UAE University and the American University of Sharjah, before Year 11 locks the choice.

faqs.question: Do your tutors cover both Cambridge and Edexcel IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the distinction matters more than parents expect. Cambridge 0580 Mathematics and Edexcel 4MA1 Mathematics A cover similar content with different paper structures, mark allocations and question styles, and the two boards tier differently. Edexcel also runs a January series, which Cambridge does not, making it the practical route for a retake that cannot wait a year. Ask your child's school which board and which tier they are entered for, and give us the code — 0580, 0625, 0620 or 4MA1 — at the enquiry stage, because the match is made on the paper rather than on the subject name.

faqs.question: Does the shortened Ramadan school day change our session time in Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: It usually does, and agreeing the change before the month begins beats improvising in its first week. School hours shorten, the family evening reshapes around Iftar, and most UAQ students switch to a later slot after the meal or to an early-afternoon slot on a reduced school day. Because lessons are online there is no travel to rearrange around either option. The calendar point is bigger than the timing one: Ramadan falls only weeks before the May IB session and the June IGCSE series, so a revision plan that ignores the month loses weeks it never counted.

faqs.question: What happens if no tutor is available for my child's subject?
faqs.answer: We say so, and say when one is expected, instead of filling the slot with a generalist. The honest gaps are the less common Diploma languages, Arabic at Diploma level and a handful of Higher Level options. The common subjects are covered: Maths AA and AI, the three sciences, Economics, Business Management, English A, and Cambridge and Edexcel IGCSE across the board. Where a subject is unavailable we will usually suggest what can be done meanwhile, such as technique work with a tutor from a neighbouring subject, and we will name that as a stopgap rather than a match.

faqs.question: My child's exams are six weeks away, so is it too late to start?
faqs.answer: Not pointless, but the work changes shape. At six weeks a tutor is triaging rather than teaching a syllabus: a diagnostic on a recent marked paper, three topics chosen by mark yield, then timed past-paper practice against the official scheme. Internal Assessment marks are already banked by then, so the focus is entirely the written papers and command-term reading, which is where students in this emirate drop the easiest marks. Two sessions a week is the usual shape at that range. Nobody can predict what grade that produces, and a provider who does is worth questioning.

faqs.question: How do I check a school's inspection report before moving my child?
faqs.answer: In Dubai you would open the KHDA report. For Umm Al Quwain, ask the school for its most recent Ministry of Education inspection outcome, the date of it, and the actions it was asked to take. Then ask the three questions an inspection report rarely answers: which Higher Levels run as separate classes rather than combined with Standard Level, how many students are in each, and whether the subject teacher has taken a cohort through a May session. Those answers tell you more about whether your child will need support than the overall band does.

umm-al-quwain.closingHeading: Start with the paper, not the postcode
umm-al-quwain.closingBody: If your child is in a Diploma or IGCSE year and something is slipping, the useful first message is specific: the school they commute to, the board, the subject, the tier or level, and what the last marked paper actually said. From Umm Al Quwain that detail matters more than location, because the tutor who fixes it is matched on the syllabus and teaches over live video rather than being drawn from the small pool living within a drive of Al Salamah. The first session is a diagnostic and the trial lesson is free, so the cost of finding out whether a match is right is one evening. Say if Arabic, Islamic Studies or a Ramadan timetable is part of the picture, because it changes the plan.

intro.heading: Al Raas households are studying in two languages and two curricula at once
paragraphs: Al Raas is the old quarter of Umm Al Quwain, on the peninsula by the historic harbour, near the fort and the pearling-town remains that gave this emirate its original economy. It is one of the most settled parts of the country: family homes held across generations, Emirati and long-resident Arabic-speaking households, and a quieter rhythm than anywhere on the Dubai side of the mountains. It is also, for schooling purposes, a long way from anything international.

That produces a household pattern this market almost never writes about. The children attend a school in Ajman, Sharjah or Ras Al Khaimah, where teaching is in English and the curriculum is British or International Baccalaureate. At the same time they sit Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies under the national requirement, taught in Arabic, assessed in their own right and appearing on the same report card. Two curricula, two languages of instruction, one week.

The consequences are specific and they are not about effort. A student whose home language is Arabic and whose school language is English carries a translation cost in every written subject, which shows up as lost marks on register and structure rather than on knowledge. A student in the Arabic first-language stream is sitting a genuinely demanding literature and grammar course, not a soft option. And the mandatory subjects take real hours from a week that already has a cross-emirate commute in it.

There is one more consequence that reaches further than any of them. Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track counts five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. A student relying on Arabic as one of their five therefore does not have five countable subjects. That is a Year 9 options decision that surfaces as a Year 13 administrative crisis, and almost nobody mentions it in Year 9.

IB Gram works across both halves of this week. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered online, one to one, over live video, and home visits are a service offered only in India. In this emirate that is the only practical arrangement: there is no resident pool of Diploma Higher Level specialists, and the Arabic first-language teacher who suits a particular school's prescribed content is unlikely to live within twenty minutes of the harbour.

What follows is written for these households. It covers who actually lives here and what each pattern needs, the real difference between the two Arabic streams, how Islamic Education and Social Studies are organised and what may and may not be taught in support, the equivalency rules in full, where marks go when a student studies in a second language, and what the double load does to a timetable.

Students attend school in another emirate in English while sitting the national subjects in Arabic

umm-al-quwain/al-raas.programmesIntro: Whichever international programme a student follows, the national subjects run alongside it. The programme determines how much room is left for them, which is the practical question for a household here.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Eight to ten externally examined subjects at the end of Year 11. Cambridge offers Arabic as a first language under code 0508 and Arabic as a foreign language under 0544, which are separate qualifications rather than tiers of one. Many UAE schools enter students for one of these alongside the school's own national-curriculum Arabic provision.
programmes.countryNote: The equivalency rule bites hardest here. Five accredited subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3 are required, and Arabic and Islamic education do not count towards them. For an Al Raas student that means the international option block has to carry five countable subjects on its own, which should be checked when Year 9 choices are made rather than discovered later.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects across Higher and Standard Level with Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Arabic can be taken within the programme as a language A or language B depending on the student's level, and the choice between those two has consequences for both workload and the grade available.
programmes.countryNote: No Ministry of Education points threshold for IB equivalency has been confirmed from an official source in the research behind this page, so none is published here. A household planning a UAE university application from the Diploma should confirm the current position on moe.gov.ae or with the emirate attestation authority rather than relying on any summary, including this one.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each and reported as criterion levels. Language acquisition and language and literature are separate groups, and the placement a school makes for an Arabic-speaking student entering an English-medium programme has effects that persist for years.
programmes.countryNote: This is the stage at which stream placements are usually made and almost never reviewed. Ask which Arabic stream the school has assigned, on what basis, and what the route out of it looks like, because a placement made administratively in Year 7 is frequently still in place in Year 11 after the student's position has changed completely.

programmes.name: International AS and A Level
programmes.description: Three or four externally examined subjects with no central core. Lighter in total workload than the Diploma, which for a student also carrying national subjects and a long commute is a genuine practical advantage rather than a lesser choice.
programmes.countryNote: The British-track equivalency requirement at this stage is one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, on top of the five IGCSE subjects. Confirm the current rule on the Ministry's own pages before fixing post-16 choices.

umm-al-quwain/al-raas.subjectsIntro: This list reflects what households in this quarter actually ask for, which includes the national subjects as often as the international ones. Each note says what the assessment rewards.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: Comprehension of unseen classical and modern texts, grammar, and extended writing in Standard Arabic. A demanding literature and language course rather than a home-language formality. Marks are lost in grammatical accuracy and structural control in extended writing far more often than in comprehension.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Functional reading, listening, controlled writing and speaking for students who did not begin in Arabic. A separate course from the first-language stream with different expectations and material. Students who read through transliteration rather than the script plateau early and do not recover without deliberate reading work.

subjects.name: Islamic Education, Arab stream
subjects.description: A timetabled and assessed subject taught in Standard Arabic for Arab students. The prescribed content may not be substituted or supplemented without prior Ministry permission, so legitimate support means teaching that content more effectively rather than offering alternative material.

subjects.name: Islamic Education, non-Arab stream
subjects.description: The same subject taught in the school's licensed curriculum language for non-Arab students, in classes organised separately from the Arab stream. Support work is comprehension and written structure within the prescribed content, which is where most of the recoverable marks sit.

subjects.name: UAE Social Studies
subjects.description: UAE history, geography and civics taught with Arabic as the primary language for Arab students. Structured extended answers and source handling carry the marks, and students who treat the subject as recall lose the organisation marks that essay planning would have earned.

subjects.name: Moral, Social and Cultural studies
subjects.description: Delivered in the school's licensed curriculum language for non-Arab students, covering values, civics and UAE context. Assessed through written work, so the gains come from paragraph planning and evidence use rather than from additional content.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Guided analysis, comparative essay, the individual oral and the Higher Level essay. For a student whose home language is not English, the first priority is analytical register rather than vocabulary breadth, because the marks reward how meaning is discussed rather than how elaborately.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Reading, writing, listening and in some variants speaking. Writing marks reward register and task fulfilment as much as accuracy, so a fluent answer in the wrong register loses marks that were plainly available. Timed writing with marked feedback is the efficient route.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE 0580 and 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The subject least affected by language of instruction and therefore the one where a bilingual student most often outperforms their report. Where marks are lost it is usually in worded multi-stage problems, which is a reading task disguised as a mathematics one.

subjects.name: Sciences (IGCSE 0620, 0625 and 0610)
subjects.description: Chemistry, physics and biology at Core and Extended tier. Command-term response is where second-language students lose the most, because an accurate description earns nothing extra when the question asked for an explanation, and the distinction is linguistic as much as scientific.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebra, functions, calculus and proof with a non-calculator paper and the Higher Level problem-solving paper. Needs long uninterrupted sessions, which in this emirate means a weekend morning rather than the tail of a commuting weekday.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0450 and 0455
subjects.description: Case study and data-response assessment where application to the stimulus material carries the marks. A strong conceptual answer that never engages with the specific case reads as competent and scores in the lower bands, which is a structural habit rather than a knowledge gap.

umm-al-quwain/al-raas.regionsTitle: Al Raas and the rest of Umm Al Quwain
umm-al-quwain/al-raas.regionsIntro: These notes describe the households in each part of the emirate and what they tend to need, because in a small settled community the pressure points differ by street in a way they do not in a new development.

regions.name: Al Raas
regions.note: The old peninsula quarter by the historic harbour and the fort. Long-settled Emirati and Arabic-speaking family homes, where students typically study in English at a school in another emirate while sitting the national subjects in Arabic.

regions.name: Umm Al Quwain old harbour and pearling quarter
regions.note: The heritage core immediately around Al Raas. Households here have the longest roots in the emirate and the furthest journey to an international curriculum, which is a combination found almost nowhere else in the country.

regions.name: Al Salamah
regions.note: The broad modern residential district inland. A higher proportion of newer arrivals and rented housing, so the typical enquiry there is about cost and transition rather than about language streams.

regions.name: UAQ Marina
regions.note: Waterfront development near the creek, with a mix of newer households. Shares the cross-emirate school run with Al Raas, so the compressed evening is identical even where the academic pressure points differ.

regions.name: Al Riqqa
regions.note: South along the coast towards Ajman. Shorter run to the Ajman schools than from the peninsula, which for some households is the difference between a sixty-minute and a forty-five-minute session being viable.

regions.name: Khor Al Beidah and Al Sinniyah
regions.note: The mangrove and island edge of the emirate. Named because the national Social Studies curriculum covers exactly this kind of local geography and history, which makes the subject unusually concrete for students who live beside it.

regions.name: Ajman
regions.note: The nearest international schooling option and the shortest cross-border run. The common choice for younger children from the peninsula for that reason alone.

regions.name: Sharjah city
regions.note: The widest school choice within reach, including IB continuum provision, and the longest routine journey. Households choosing it accept a shorter evening in exchange for a wider option block.

schoolClusters.city: Schools in Ajman and Sharjah used by Al Raas families
schoolClusters.note: Where most internationally schooled students from the peninsula attend. Every one of these schools timetables Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies alongside its licensed international curriculum, because the federal rule requires it. Schools in Sharjah sit under the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which also approves curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods.

schoolClusters.city: Umm Al Quwain and the northern option
schoolClusters.note: Private schools within Umm Al Quwain are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education, and the emirate's international provision is limited. Families also look north, where Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge regulates private education and approves fees, curricula and assessment methods in that emirate.

sections.heading: Who lives in Al Raas and what each household needs first
paragraphs: This quarter is not a mixed new development and it does not behave like one. The households are mostly settled, often multi-generational, and the schooling question is usually not whether to use an international curriculum but how to carry it alongside a national one. The variable that predicts the academic pressure point better than anything else is which language is spoken at home relative to which language the school teaches in.

An Arabic-speaking household with children in an English-medium school is carrying the heavier version of the arrangement. The student is reasoning in one language and being assessed in another in every written subject, and that cost appears as marks lost on register, structure and command-term response rather than on understanding. The same student is often genuinely strong in mathematics, which is the subject least affected by the language of assessment, and that gap between subjects is the diagnostic signal.

A household where English is the home language has the mirror problem: the national subjects are the difficult half. Arabic as an additional language, Islamic Education taught in the school's curriculum language, and Moral, Social and Cultural studies are examined subjects with their own homework and reports, and treating them as background noise is how a report card acquires its weakest line.

The third pattern is a student in the Arabic first-language stream who is being under-served by the assumption that it is easy for them. First-language Arabic is a demanding literature and grammar course, and a fluent speaker can sit comfortably in the middle of it without specific work on grammatical accuracy and structural control in extended writing. The table below sorts these patterns and names the first useful action for each.

sections.heading: The two Arabic courses, and why they are not two levels
paragraphs: Schools in the UAE run Arabic as two distinct provisions, and families frequently talk about them as though one were the advanced version of the other. They are different courses with different content, different assessment and different purposes, and placing a student in the wrong one is a mistake that compounds every year it is not corrected.

Arabic as a first language assesses comprehension of unseen classical and modern texts, grammar and extended writing in Standard Arabic. It is taught in Standard Arabic and it is a literature and language course in the full sense. Cambridge offers a first-language Arabic qualification under code 0508. Arabic as an additional language assesses functional reading, listening, controlled writing and speaking for students who did not begin in Arabic, with Cambridge's foreign-language syllabus under code 0544.

The organisation of these classes is not left to a school's discretion. Published guidance requires schools to organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and states that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language.

For support, the practical rule is that material written for one stream is the wrong material for the other. A first-language student needs grammar and structural control work on extended writing; an additional-language student needs script fluency and vocabulary retention through short frequent practice. Ask the school which stream your child is in and on what basis, because the placement is often made administratively on entry and rarely revisited.

sections.heading: Islamic Education, Social Studies and what support may legitimately cover
paragraphs: No competing page in this market has a section on these subjects, which is remarkable given that every private-school student in the country takes some version of them. The federal position is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Published guidance for Dubai sets out the operational detail, and it is the clearest public reference available.

Several of those details constrain what honest support looks like. Classes must be organised separately for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes are strictly prohibited. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and Arabic is the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, while the school's licensed curriculum language is used for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

The most important constraint for anyone offering support is this: for these subjects the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry, is strictly prohibited. That rules out alternative syllabuses, imported material and anybody's own version of the course. Legitimate support means teaching the prescribed content more effectively, which in practice is comprehension, recall structure and written organisation. The guidance also notes that teaching time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, that schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and that any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least twenty-five minutes.

One further point is a useful check on any provider. The guidance requires schools to ensure that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate regulator approval to teach those subjects. That is a school-level requirement rather than a tutoring one, but it indicates how specific the expectations are, and a provider who treats these subjects as interchangeable with any Arabic lesson has not read them.

sections.heading: The equivalency rules in full, and the number that catches families out
paragraphs: Equivalency turns a foreign school certificate into a document a UAE institution will accept. It is administered by the Ministry of Education, no tutoring provider performs or guarantees it, and the published requirements are specific enough that a family can plan around them if they read them in time. Most do not, which is why the subject count is the single most common late discovery in households like these.

On the British track a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five required subjects. On top of that they must show one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. At least one page currently ranking for these queries publishes a six-subject requirement, which is not what the published guidance says; publishing the correct number is a small factual advantage and a large practical one.

On the American track the thresholds are test-based. English proficiency requires a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT. Mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. The published guidance makes no mention of a UAE-specific national test for this purpose, and it states no International Baccalaureate points threshold, so none is published here.

The planning consequence for an Al Raas household is concrete. If a student's option block contains five international subjects plus Arabic plus Islamic Education, they have five countable subjects only if all five international subjects are passed at the required grade. Dropping one in Year 10 removes the margin entirely. Check the count when options are chosen, and confirm the current rule on moe.gov.ae rather than relying on any summary.

sections.heading: Studying in a second language: where the marks actually go
paragraphs: A student reasoning in Arabic and writing in English does not have a knowledge problem, and treating it as one wastes a term. The losses are linguistic and they are concentrated in specific, teachable places. Identifying them from marked work rather than from a report grade is the difference between four sessions and a year of general English support that was never the right product.

The clearest signal is a gap between mathematics and the written subjects. Mathematics is the subject least mediated by the language of assessment, so a bilingual student who sits comfortably above target there and below target in biology and geography is telling you something precise. The second signal is half-earned long questions: answers that are accurate, relevant and still short of the marks because the response shape did not match the command term.

Command terms are where most of the recoverable marks sit. Describe asks what; explain asks why with a causal link; evaluate asks for competing positions weighed and a judgement reached. A student whose English is functional but not analytical reads all three as an invitation to write about the topic, and loses marks in every section of every paper in a way that looks like inconsistency rather than a pattern. Sorting past-paper questions by command term and writing one-line answer plans is the efficient fix.

Register and task fulfilment are the other half, and they are assessed explicitly in English papers and implicitly everywhere else. A student who writes a fluent, warm, personal answer where a formal analytical one was wanted loses marks that vocabulary work would never have recovered. This is why second-language support should be built on the student's own science and humanities answers rather than taught as a general English course.

sections.heading: The double load and what it does to a week
paragraphs: Add it up for a student from this quarter. A cross-emirate journey to Ajman, Sharjah or Ras Al Khaimah and back. A full international curriculum with homework. Arabic in whichever stream the school assigned, with its own homework and assessments. Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies, timetabled and examined. For a Diploma student, coursework produced entirely outside lesson time. That is a heavier week than most study plans assume.

The common failure is a plan that allocates hours to the international subjects and treats the national subjects as something that happens by itself. It does not, and the report card will eventually say so. The honest version allocates time to both halves, which usually means supporting fewer international subjects properly rather than more of them thinly, and that is an uncomfortable conversation worth having early.

Session design has to reflect the fatigue as well as the hours. A student home at five after a Sharjah run is not capable of the same work at six as a student who walked home at three, and buying ninety minutes of their attention at that hour is buying a tired version of a good session. Short weekday slots with one objective, long work moved to Saturday morning, is the pattern that holds here across a full term.

In Ramadan the whole structure changes, and for households in this quarter it changes more than most because the national subjects and the religious calendar interact. Afternoons become unproductive, post-Iftar hours become the useful ones, and new abstract content is better moved out of the period entirely in favour of consolidation and past-paper review. Rewrite the plan for the month rather than carrying it through unchanged.

sections.heading: Who supervises schooling here, and what MoE supervision means
paragraphs: Families in this emirate who read national coverage of school inspections sometimes wonder why they never see a rating for their own school. The answer is structural. Umm Al Quwain's private schools are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education, which in the government's own words plays a supervisory role over private schools in the emirates of Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. There is no emirate-level authority here publishing an annual band.

For most Al Raas households the more relevant regulator is the one covering the school the child actually attends, which is usually in another emirate. A Sharjah school falls under the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which regulates private education there and approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods. A Ras Al Khaimah school falls under the Department of Knowledge with comparable powers. Those are substantive differences, not naming differences.

What no regulator does is accredit tutoring providers. Individual private tutors in the UAE need the private tuition work permit introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation and granted free of charge for two years, with a stated completion time of two working days. A tutoring operation with premises and staff needs a separate educational services permit. Anyone describing themselves as approved by an education regulator should be asked which document they actually hold.

The federal curriculum baseline underpins everything above: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That single sentence is the reason a British-curriculum school in Ajman timetables the same national subjects as a government school down the road from Al Raas.

sections.heading: Starting from Al Raas, in the right order
paragraphs: The first two things to establish are not about tutoring at all. Find out which Arabic stream the school has placed your child in and on what basis, and count how many countable subjects their option block will produce for equivalency. Both are single emails and both can save a great deal of money and difficulty later. Neither is something a tutoring provider should be deciding for you.

Then the practical specifics. The subject, the board, the syllabus code, the tier where one applies, the level, the real arrival time at home after the commute, and one recent piece of marked work from a written subject rather than from mathematics. That last detail matters, because the marked written answer is where a second-language pattern shows up and a mathematics paper will not reveal it.

The first lesson is free and diagnostic. For a household here it is usually spent working out which of the two halves of the week is actually costing the marks, and whether the loss is linguistic or genuine subject content. It ends with a short written note naming the gap, the session format that fits the evening, and how many sessions the work should take. That note is useful whether or not anything is booked.

On availability, the honest position in this emirate is that narrow Higher Level specialists and specific Arabic first-language teachers may not be free at the late hour a commuting household needs. In that case you should get a timeline and alternative slots rather than a substitute. And if a match is wrong after two or three sessions, the tutor is changed, because an evening this short is too scarce to spend on a pairing that is not working.

process.title: Check the Arabic stream first
process.description: Ask the school which stream your child is in, on what basis, and what moving between them would involve. Placements are usually made administratively on entry and rarely reviewed, and material written for one stream is the wrong material for the other.

process.title: Count the equivalency subjects
process.description: Five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at grade E or 3 are required and Arabic and Islamic education do not count towards them. Count what the option block will actually produce, and do it when choices are made rather than in Year 13.

process.title: Send a marked written answer
process.description: A marked science or humanities answer shows a second-language pattern that a mathematics paper hides. Add the board, syllabus code and tier, and one line on any pattern you have noticed yourself.

process.title: Give the real arrival time
process.description: Tell us when your child genuinely gets home after the journey from Ajman, Sharjah or Ras Al Khaimah, including bus stops. That sets the session length, and getting it wrong is the usual reason a plan lasts three weeks here.

process.title: Take the free trial and decide after it
process.description: The first lesson costs nothing and works out which half of the week is costing the marks and whether the loss is linguistic or content. It ends with a written note naming the gap and a session count you can act on independently.

whyPoints.title: Both halves of the week are covered
whyPoints.description: The national subjects are examined, reported and real, and they are treated that way here rather than left out of the plan. Arabic is taught in the stream the school assigned, and national-subject support stays strictly inside the prescribed content.

whyPoints.title: The two Arabic streams are not confused
whyPoints.description: First-language Arabic is a literature and grammar course; additional-language Arabic is an acquisition course. They need different material, different session patterns and different tutors, and the distinction is made before any session is booked.

whyPoints.title: The equivalency count published plainly
whyPoints.description: Five accredited subjects at grade E or 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded. At least one competing page publishes a six-subject requirement; the published guidance says five, and we say so and point to the official source.

whyPoints.title: Second-language losses diagnosed, not guessed
whyPoints.description: A gap between mathematics and written subjects is a specific diagnostic signal, not a general ability finding. Support is built on the student's own science and humanities answers rather than sold as a general English course.

whyPoints.title: Designed for a commuting evening
whyPoints.description: Short weekday sessions with one objective, long work on a Saturday morning. Lessons are taught live online, one to one, so nothing depends on anyone driving to the peninsula at the end of the working day.

whyPoints.title: No regulator claimed as a credential
whyPoints.description: No education authority in the UAE accredits tutoring providers. Individual tutors hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, free for two years, and that is the document to ask for.

faqs.question: Does Arabic count towards the five subjects needed for equivalency?
faqs.answer: No, and neither does Islamic education. The published guidance requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, and states that Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. For an Al Raas household that means the international option block has to produce five countable passes on its own, so a student with five international subjects plus Arabic plus Islamic Education has no margin at all if one of the five is dropped or failed. Confirm the current rule on moe.gov.ae.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE subjects does a student in the UAE actually need?
faqs.answer: The published guidance states five accredited subjects at no less than grade E or grade 3 for the GCSE and IGCSE stage of the British track, excluding Arabic and Islamic education from that count. At least one page currently ranking for these queries publishes a six-subject requirement, which does not match the published guidance. Schools often enter students for eight to ten subjects for other reasons, including university competitiveness, but the equivalency floor is five countable ones. Verify the current position on moe.gov.ae before planning around either number.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Arabic as a first language and as an additional language?
faqs.answer: They are separate courses, not two levels of one. First-language Arabic assesses comprehension of unseen classical and modern texts, grammar and extended writing in Standard Arabic, with Cambridge offering it under code 0508. Additional-language Arabic assesses functional reading, listening, controlled writing and speaking for students who did not begin in Arabic, with Cambridge's foreign-language syllabus under 0544. Published guidance requires schools to run them as separate classes and prohibits combined classes for Arab and non-Arab students, because expectations and language of instruction differ.

faqs.question: Our child is a fluent Arabic speaker but only getting middling grades in Arabic. Why?
faqs.answer: Because the first-language course is a literature and grammar qualification rather than a test of conversational fluency. Marks are lost in grammatical accuracy and structural control in extended writing far more often than in comprehension, and a fluent speaker can sit comfortably in the middle of the course without ever working on those. Treat it as you would English Literature for a native English speaker: a subject with technical demands that need teaching. One longer weekly session on writing structure usually moves it more than general reading practice.

faqs.question: Can a tutor teach a different Islamic Education syllabus if my child is struggling?
faqs.answer: No. The published guidance for the mandatory UAE subjects states that the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry, is strictly prohibited. Legitimate support means teaching the prescribed content more effectively: comprehension, recall structure and written organisation within it. Which stream your child is in also governs the language of instruction, since Islamic Education is taught in Standard Arabic for Arab students and in the school's licensed curriculum language for non-Arab students. Any provider offering an alternative course has not read the rules.

faqs.question: Why does the school run separate Arabic and Islamic Education classes?
faqs.answer: Because it is required to. Published guidance states that for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and that combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited due to the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, with Arabic the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students and the school's curriculum language used for non-Arabs.

faqs.question: My child is strong in maths and weak in biology and geography. What does that mean?
faqs.answer: It is usually a language-of-assessment signal rather than an ability one. Mathematics is the subject least mediated by the language a student writes in, so a bilingual student above target in maths and below target in written subjects is pointing at a specific, teachable problem: command-term response, register and answer structure. The efficient fix is work on their own marked science and humanities answers rather than a general English course, and it is typically four to six sessions rather than a term of broad support.

faqs.question: How do command terms cost a second-language student marks?
faqs.answer: By looking like synonyms when they are not. Describe asks what happened; explain asks why, with an explicit causal link; evaluate asks for competing positions weighed and a judgement reached. A student whose English is functional but not analytical reads all three as an invitation to write about the topic, and loses marks in every section of every paper, which looks like inconsistency rather than a pattern. Sorting twenty past-paper questions by command term and writing one-line answer plans moves more marks than any amount of extra content revision.

faqs.question: Is there an IB points requirement for UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: None was confirmed from an official Ministry source in the research behind this page, so none is published here. The British-track and American-track requirements are published and appear on this page; the IB figure is not among them. Anyone quoting a specific IB points threshold should be asked where they read it. Confirm the current position on moe.gov.ae or with the emirate attestation authority, or ask your school's IB coordinator, who deals with the process for every graduating cohort and will have the current position.

faqs.question: How long is a mandatory-subject lesson supposed to be?
faqs.answer: Published guidance calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a forty-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least twenty-five minutes. The practical use of knowing that is budgeting your child's week honestly: these are timetabled, examined subjects with homework attached, and a study plan that allocates every spare hour to IGCSE revision has not counted the whole load the student is actually carrying.

faqs.question: Which regulator covers a school in Umm Al Quwain?
faqs.answer: The federal Ministry of Education, which plays a supervisory role over private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. There is no emirate-level authority here publishing an annual inspection band, which is why families never see a rating for a school in this emirate. For most Al Raas households the relevant regulator is the one covering the school the child actually attends in another emirate: the Sharjah Private Education Authority, or Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge, both of which also approve fees, curricula and assessment methods.

faqs.question: Can the national subjects and the international curriculum both be supported?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for a household here that is usually the right allocation. The practical pattern is two short slots a week rather than one long one: one on an international subject and one on Arabic or a national subject, with national-subject work staying strictly inside the prescribed content. The alternative, which is what most plans do, is to allocate everything to the international curriculum and let the national subjects produce the weakest line on the report card. Supporting fewer international subjects properly is the trade worth making.

faqs.question: What time can a session run from the peninsula on a school night?
faqs.answer: Later than most families estimate. A student travelling back from Sharjah city on a bus with stops is often not home before five, which puts a workable start at around 6.30pm, and from Ajman closer to 5.30pm. At that hour a forty-five minute session with a single named objective holds, where ninety minutes buys a tired version of a good lesson. Long work belongs on a Saturday morning with no commute behind the student. In Ramadan, move to a shorter post-Iftar slot instead.

faqs.question: Should we ask the school to change the Arabic stream?
faqs.answer: First ask which stream your child is in and on what basis, because the placement is often made administratively on entry and rarely reviewed even after the student's position changes. The two streams are different courses with different assessment, so the question is which course fits now rather than which one is harder. Ask what moving would involve and when a move is possible in the school's cycle. It is a school decision, not something a tutoring provider should influence, and the answer should be in writing.

faqs.question: Is online teaching workable for Arabic and the national subjects?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in this emirate it is the only reliable option. There is no resident pool of specialists here, so a teacher matched to the specific stream and the school's prescribed content is unlikely to live nearby. Screen sharing suits script work, grammar annotation and written structure well, because both people see the same text with the same marks on it. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; lessons are taught live online, one to one, with the first one free and a written diagnosis at the end of it.

umm-al-quwain/al-raas.closingHeading: Start with the stream and the subject count, then book the trial
umm-al-quwain/al-raas.closingBody: For a household in Al Raas the two highest-value questions cost nothing: which Arabic stream has the school assigned and on what basis, and how many countable subjects will the option block actually produce for equivalency. Ask those by email first. Then send the subject, the board, the syllabus code, the tier, the real arrival time after the commute, and one marked answer from a written subject rather than from mathematics. The first lesson is free, taught online one to one over live video, and ends with a written note on which half of the week is costing the marks and how many sessions it should take.

umm-al-quwain/al-riqqa.tutorsIntro: The tutors below cover Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE and the IB Diploma and Middle Years Programme. Each takes one student at a time and works on the independent half of the course rather than re-teaching the lesson the student already attended.

intro.heading: School sets the work; nobody at home checks whether it was done properly
paragraphs: Al Riqqa runs south along the Umm Al Quwain coast towards Ajman, which makes it the part of this emirate with the shortest cross-border school run. Families here send children to Ajman and Sharjah schools and get them back earlier than households on the peninsula do. That should be an advantage, and it is, but it exposes a different problem rather than removing one: the hours are available and nobody is supervising what happens in them.

A school teaches the syllabus and sets homework. What it also does, invisibly, is assume. It assumes a student will mark their own practice honestly against a scheme rather than glancing at the answer. It assumes they will accumulate past-paper volume rather than reading worked examples. It assumes a returned mock script will be analysed rather than filed. It assumes revision will be sequenced and spaced rather than crammed. None of those assumptions is unreasonable and almost none of them holds without being taught.

That is why a conscientious student can sit in every lesson, finish every set task and still arrive at a grade that nobody can explain. The teaching happened. The independent work happened, in the sense that time was spent. What did not happen was the part that converts time into marks, and in most schools nobody is scheduled to teach it because it is not on any syllabus.

In Umm Al Quwain the gap is wider than average for a structural reason. The emirate has limited international school provision, so students travel out, and a commuting student has less informal contact with teachers: no lingering after class, no catching a teacher at break to ask about a mark. The written feedback that arrives by email is the whole of the information flow, which places more weight on the student's own ability to read and act on it.

There is a second structural reason the gap is wide here. Umm Al Quwain has no emirate-level education authority publishing annual inspection outcomes; its private schools are supervised by the federal Ministry of Education, which performs that role for Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. Families therefore have fewer public reference points for judging how much a school is doing beyond the taught timetable, and more of the judgement about independent work falls back on the household itself.

IB Gram works on that half. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered online, one to one, over live video, and home visits are a service offered only in India. The format suits this work particularly well, because self-marking, past-paper analysis and mock review are all document-based: both people look at the same script with the same annotations, which is more precise than the same conversation across a table.

What follows audits the week honestly, sets out how to teach self-marking, gives a past-paper schedule by stage of year, puts the Cambridge and Pearson series calendars side by side, explains how to extract the data a mock actually contains, and covers the self-study and external-candidate routes for a subject a local school cannot offer.

umm-al-quwain/al-riqqa.programmesIntro: How much a programme assumes a student will manage alone differs sharply between the three routes below, and so does the kind of independent work that matters.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Terminal examinations at the end of Year 11 across eight to ten subjects. The independent demand here is almost entirely volume and self-marking: practice accumulated over months and checked honestly against published schemes. Cambridge separates Core and Extended tiers in several subjects, so practice must match the tier the school entered.
programmes.countryNote: Confirming the board, the code, the tier and the series by email matters more for a commuting family, because nobody is at the school gate to ask informally. Get it in writing in Year 10 and keep it, since every past paper the student touches for two years depends on that answer being right.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. The independent demand is coursework as well as revision, and it runs continuously rather than peaking before exams. Internal assessments are produced outside lesson time and submitted to internal deadlines set months before the written papers.
programmes.countryNote: A Diploma student commuting out of Umm Al Quwain has the hardest version of this, because coursework deadlines fall in the same evenings as homework and the travel has already taken part of the week. Front-loading coursework in Year 12 is the only version of the plan that works, and it has to be set up deliberately in September.

programmes.name: International AS and A Level
programmes.description: Three or four externally examined subjects with no central core. The independent expectation shifts towards reading beyond the lesson and sustained past-paper work, and the modular structure differs between boards, which affects when a result can be banked and therefore when a subject stops consuming revision time.
programmes.countryNote: With fewer subjects and no coursework core, A Levels are the more forgiving route for a commuting student, but they assume more unprompted reading. A student used to being told exactly what to study will find the first set of internal exams unpleasant unless that habit is built deliberately in the first term.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four criteria each and reported as criterion levels from 0 to 8. The independent demand is modest but the habits formed here are the ones the Diploma will rely on, particularly keeping a process journal and reading criterion feedback rather than the summary grade.
programmes.countryNote: Ask the school for the criterion-level breakdown rather than the summary grade. For a commuting household it is the cheapest and most informative diagnostic available, it arrives by email, and it is the earliest warning of the independent-work habits that will cost marks in the Diploma.

umm-al-quwain/al-riqqa.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are listed by what independent work actually moves them, because that is where the assumed hours either pay off or do not.

subjects.name: Mathematics (IGCSE 0580 and 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The purest volume subject. Thirty mixed multi-stage questions a week, self-marked against the scheme, moves a grade in a term. Reading worked examples for the same number of hours does not, and the difference between the two is invisible to anyone watching the student at a desk.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebra, functions, calculus and proof with a non-calculator paper and the Higher Level problem-solving paper. Independent work has to include attempting questions that defeat the student, because the Higher Level paper rewards sustaining an argument rather than recognising a type.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0625 and 4PH1
subjects.description: Multi-step questions are the grade boundary. Independent practice should be deliberately mixed rather than organised by topic, because selecting between energy, momentum and force approaches is the skill, and a topic-labelled exercise removes the selection step entirely.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0620 and 4CH1
subjects.description: Practical-reasoning questions about apparatus, anomalous readings and improvements are examined on the written paper and almost never revised deliberately, because they do not look like content. They are among the most recoverable marks available to an independent student.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0610 and 4BI1
subjects.description: Command-term discipline is the whole of the independent gain. A student who sorts past questions by command term and writes one-line answer plans learns more in an hour than one who rereads a chapter, and the effect carries across every paper in the subject.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: Independent work means timed writing that someone marks, which is precisely the part a student cannot supply alone. Where no marking is available, comparing their own answer against a published model line by line is the usable substitute.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Planning rather than writing is the efficient independent task. Five essay plans in an hour teaches more about argument structure than one finished essay, and the individual oral rewards rehearsal, which is one of the few genuinely solo activities on the course.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0450 and 0455
subjects.description: Case-study application is learned by doing many short case questions rather than by learning more theory. The evaluation marks at the end of long questions are the most commonly abandoned on the paper and the most improvable without a teacher present.

subjects.name: Geography and History
subjects.levels: IB HL and SL, IGCSE 0460 and 0470
subjects.description: Case-study deployment and source handling. Independent work should be practising the deployment rather than accumulating more case material, because students almost always know more than they can use under time pressure.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Tracing algorithms by hand under time pressure is the examined skill most neglected by independent study, because writing code on a machine feels more productive and tests something different from what the paper asks for.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Retention-led, so independent work has to be frequent and short rather than long and weekly. Fifteen minutes daily on script reading and vocabulary beats a two-hour Saturday session, and the difference shows within a month.

subjects.name: Coursework and internal assessment
subjects.description: The work most exposed by a lack of supervision, because deadlines are internal and nobody chases until late. Independent progress depends on reading the criteria against the student's own draft, which is a teachable step and almost never taught.

sections.heading: Auditing the week: taught hours against assumed hours
paragraphs: The useful first exercise is an hours audit rather than a subject review. Write down, for one real week, how many hours the student spends in taught lessons, how many on set homework, and how many on work that nobody set but everybody assumes: revision, past papers, coursework, reading. The third column is usually the largest for a Year 11 or Year 13 student and the only one with no supervision attached.

From Al Riqqa that third column is genuinely available, which is the local advantage. The Ajman run is short, students are home early by this emirate's standards, and the afternoon is not consumed by travel the way it is on the peninsula. Having the hours and not converting them is a more frustrating problem than not having them, and it is also a more fixable one.

What the audit usually reveals is that the assumed hours are being spent on the lowest-return activities. Rereading notes, copying out summaries, reorganising files, watching explanation videos. All of those feel like study, produce a visible artefact, and return very little per hour compared with timed retrieval, mixed-topic practice and self-marked past-paper work. The student is not idle; they are busy at the wrong things.

There is a second reason the audit is worth doing in writing rather than in your head. Independent hours are the part of the week nobody reports on, so a household's sense of them comes from impressions: the student was at the desk, the door was shut, the light was on. An hours table makes the distinction between presence and activity visible, and it usually settles an argument that was otherwise going to be had repeatedly for two years.
The table below is a template for that audit. Fill in the real numbers for one week rather than an estimate for a typical week, because estimates average away the two evenings that actually vanished.

sections.heading: Homework that is set against work that is assumed
paragraphs: Parents often judge whether a student is working by whether homework is finished, and that is a reasonable proxy for a Year 8 student and a poor one for a Year 11. Set homework is a fraction of the expected independent load by the final two years, and a student can complete all of it conscientiously while doing almost none of the work that actually determines the grade.

The distinction is worth making explicit in the household. Set homework is a floor, not a target. It is designed to consolidate the lesson, it is collected, and the student gets feedback on it. The assumed work is a different category: nobody set it, nobody collects it, and its absence shows up only in an examination months later. Treating the first as sufficient is the most common honest mistake families make.

There is a related trap in the way schools communicate. A teacher reporting that a student always finishes their homework is reporting on the floor, accurately and positively, and a parent hears a general statement about diligence. Both are behaving reasonably. The question that produces useful information is different: how much past-paper work has this student done, and have I seen any of it marked?

For a commuting household the follow-up matters more than elsewhere, because informal contact is limited. Written questions by email produce written answers, and a short specific question about independent work volume is more likely to get a useful reply than a general question about progress. The answer also tells you whether the school is tracking it at all, which is itself worth knowing.

sections.heading: Self-marking: the skill that stands in for a teacher at home
paragraphs: Of all the assumed skills, self-marking has the best return and is the least taught. A student who can take their own attempt at a long question and compare it honestly against a published mark scheme has effectively acquired a teacher for every hour of independent work they do. A student who cannot has to wait for someone else to tell them what went wrong, which in a commuting household may be a week later or never.

Doing it properly is a procedure rather than an attitude. Attempt the question under timed conditions and stop when the time stops. Mark in a different colour, awarding marks only for what is actually written rather than for what was intended. Note the mark lost and why, in a word or two, beside each loss. Then group the losses: content, method presentation, command-term response, or pacing. The grouping is the useful output and it takes two minutes.

The reason it fails without teaching is that students mark generously and do not know it. A step they were holding in their head reads as present; a conclusion they implied reads as stated. Watching a specialist mark the same script strictly, and then marking the next one themselves with the specialist questioning each awarded mark, corrects that in a handful of sessions. After that the student keeps the skill for the rest of their education.

Two cautions. Mark schemes and past papers belong to the exam boards, so they should be accessed through the school or the board's official site rather than from any provider distributing copies, and the version must match the syllabus code and series. And honesty is the whole mechanism: a self-marked score that flatters is worse than no score, because it removes the signal that something needs fixing.

sections.heading: Past papers: how many, which, and in what order
paragraphs: Past-paper practice is the highest-return independent activity in the final two years and it is almost always started too late and organised badly. Students typically begin complete papers a few weeks before the exams, having spent the preceding year on topic exercises, and discover pacing problems at the point where there is no time left to fix them.

A better sequence starts earlier and changes shape. Through the first year of a course, questions by topic, immediately after that topic is taught, are the right unit: they convert fresh teaching into exam-format practice while the content is still live. From the start of the final year, mixed-topic sets matter more, because selecting the right method is the examined skill and a topic-labelled question removes the selection. Complete papers under timed conditions belong monthly from the start of the final year and weekly in the last term.

Which papers also matters. They must match the board, the syllabus code, the tier and the current syllabus version, because a paper from an earlier specification can test content no longer on the course and omit content that is. A student practising the wrong board's papers loses marks on format rather than knowledge, which is the most avoidable loss available and is entirely a consequence of nobody having checked the code.

Marking is the constraint. A student can self-mark structured and calculation questions reliably once taught, but extended written answers need someone else, which is the sensible division of labour: volume done independently, extended writing marked by a specialist, and the session spent on what the marking revealed rather than on working through questions together.
